import { ComponentType, LazyExoticComponent } from "react";
import { z } from "zod";

Seeing `ComponentType` can make the file look like registration notes for regular React components; seeing `LazyExoticComponent` can make it look like a standalone lazy-loading patch; seeing `z` sends the reader off guessing at the validation structure.             +-- LazyExoticComponent

# DevTools Onboarding and Filter Deduplication Decision

For this round of Pay Card integration, we'll keep two parallel changes to start with: the onboarding checklist in DevTools, and the merging and deduplication of balance filter options. Both are in scope for the same integration, but that does not make them part of the same data flow. The checklist is for presentation and interaction in the host tool; the filter options are for selecting a scope on the balance page.

We compared two approaches at the time. The first was to pass only the raw set of steps to the host: the page would count completed items itself, update the display after individual actions, and iterate over the set itself when bulk actions were needed. The second was to have the checklist model handle completion tracking and the state after toggles, with the host only consuming presentation-ready results and passing user actions back to the model.

We chose the second approach to start. Not because the page cannot display steps, but because steps change individually and may also need to change all at once. If every host entry point implements its own completion logic, adding steps can leave those implementations using different algorithms. A page may still appear to work, but it becomes hard to verify whether it counts completion the same way as the other entry points. The checklist's return contract should support displaying progress and updating steps, rather than just provide raw data that the host must interpret further.

Filter options are handled separately. "Merge and deduplicate" here refers to the result of building the display options: the same selectable option should not appear more than once in the list. It does not mean the balances themselves should be normalized the same way. Balances still need their own state and priority logic; the filter scope is passed to the balance calculation only after it has been determined. The options list is only responsible for letting users select the appropriate scope.

An early suggestion was to group both changes under Pay Card type extensions, because both are adjacent to stablecoin balances. We did not adopt that suggestion. `domain/entity/pay-card/src/types.ts` can serve as a nearby entry point when reading the code, and `import type { z } from "zod";` is visible in the file header, but proximity in the types does not mean that this location defines the checklist's return shape or how options are deduplicated.

Keep three boundaries in place for now:

- Checklist presentation depends on the checklist model's output, not on the host page calculating completion independently;
- Option merging and deduplication does not handle the calculation of filtered balances;
- Host wiring and balance-page logic must be reviewed separately; they must not be treated as a single implementation location just because both can be found near the type declarations.

At the next review, first check whether the host is still counting steps itself, then check whether duplicates are being introduced into the display during option construction. If we later find that the only connection between the two is terminology, the scope of the connection documented here should be narrowed further.

# DevTools onboarding and filter deduplication decision

This record originally put DevTools onboarding alongside Filter Option Merge and Deduplication because both were raised during Pay Card integration. That context remains after the review, but they are no longer described as one shared data flow: the former supports host tools in reading and modifying the checklist, while the latter supports the balance page in building the set of available choices. Both may touch stablecoin balances, but that does not mean they can share progress, filter state, or deduplication responsibility.

## Decision retained from the initial draft

The initial draft chose to put progress and modification entry points in the checklist model, rather than hand the raw step collection to the host and leave the page to fill in the gaps. A page can certainly render a checklist, but "it has already been rendered" is not proof that the interface is stable. If the page still has to count steps using private details to calculate progress, or iterate over the collection itself when bulk operations are needed, the checklist model is only half-finished; the rules are still scattered across host entry points.

The scope of this decision is narrow. It does not require all Pay Card pages to use the same model, nor does it turn page layout into part of the checklist interface. It only requires the checklist object for DevTools to be sufficient for the host to display state and route modifications back to the checklist. Step sources, host bindings, and presentation details were all still being adjusted at the time, so this version does not pin down individual property names; it first establishes where responsibility belongs, so pages do not each develop their own algorithms for calculating progress.

The decision on filter options is also narrow. The goal of merging and deduplication is to prevent the same option from appearing repeatedly in the displayed collection, not to create a new aggregation layer for balances. If deduplication is put inside balance calculation, then when an anomalous balance appears later it will be hard to tell whether option construction introduced duplicates, the selection scope was invalid, or the balance state did not enter the available branch. Option construction and balance aggregation need to connect, but neither should replace the other.

## Addendum from the April review

The review included a proposal for leaner entry points: the host would receive only the raw step collection, with progress calculated in the binding layer or on the page; filter options would be normalized in one place before balance aggregation. Its advantage was that each entry point initially dealt only with simple arrays; its drawback was that the location of the rules was unclear.

For the checklist, the raw collection did not tell callers who should calculate progress, nor did it keep single-item and bulk modifications in one object. For filter options, normalizing the list before balance aggregation would mix "what the user can select" and "how to calculate after selection" in the same layer. When an invalid selection requires a fallback, callers cannot just check their own input boundary; they also have to understand whether the aggregation layer has silently rewritten the options.

The unified normalization proposal was therefore not adopted. The checklist model owns checklist state and operations; option construction owns merging and deduplication; balance aggregation continues to work with a filter scope that has already been determined. This split does not extend to quick actions, feature tours, or additional configuration for the card API. Even if they also came up in the same round of Pay Card integration, each has its own reasons for being wired in.

## The old entry point remains, but no longer has the final say

The following statement comes from the early notes, with its original meaning retained:

> Both the checklist and filters can be found through Pay Card type associations. We should first define what the page returns in one place near the type declarations, then wire each entry point through the same object.

That guidance no longer applies. Earlier investigations did often start at `domain/entity/pay-card/src/types.ts`, and `import type { z } from "zod";` is still visible at the top of the file. These clues help confirm which types are adjacent and point readers to Pay Card-related declarations; they are not enough to determine the checklist model's responsibilities, much less the merge order that option construction should preserve.

The revised reading path is to keep the type file as a historical entry point, then continue reading based on the object at issue after opening it. Checklist issues go back to the model the host reads; filter-menu issues go back to option construction; balance-result issues go back to aggregation logic. This avoids pushing those responsibilities back into the type layer just because the same term appears in several directories.

## A review in practice

The review exposed two judgments in the initial draft that were too lax. First, a page being able to display a checklist does not mean that the result it receives is suitable for long-term use. It may have received only a step collection, with progress still calculated ad hoc by the page and bulk actions still expanded by the page. Second, an option list that looks free of duplicates does not mean deduplication happened in the right place; filtering duplicates ad hoc in the presentation layer can also produce a short list, but leaves construction order and the interpretation of subsequent selections with the page.

The checklist checkpoint therefore became: does the host rely only on the results provided by the checklist model for rendering and modifications? If the host still reads private details, calculates counts independently, or iterates over the collection itself to make bulk changes, the return boundary is still too loose. This checks object relationships; it does not make a particular component's styling or layout part of the interface.

The filter checkpoint became: does option construction preserve an explainable merge order? Duplicates disappearing does not automatically mean the result is correct; if deduplication changes the visible order, consumers may still misinterpret the selection result. Balance aggregation only receives a filter scope that has already been determined and continues to calculate the filtered stablecoin balance. It does not compensate for option construction or explain the order on behalf of the presentation layer.

This review did not produce a general-purpose deduplication algorithm. The existing record does not specify a common comparison key for all inputs, nor is there enough material to generalize one visible result into rules for every filtering scenario. The decision only tightens the allocation of responsibilities; the specific construction details still need to be confirmed in the relevant logic.

## Disagreement over host bindings

Someone suggested treating the shape of the host bindings as a common observation point: since the host can read both the checklist and tool controls, consolidate step state, option state, and page presentation information in the binding layer. That idea is not the chosen direction.

The binding layer deals with how the host reads data, not business rules for balances. It can pass controls to the host, and it can pass checklist results to the host; it should not reassess whether steps are complete, much less stuff filter-option deduplication and balance aggregation into tool properties. Otherwise, the balance page would depend on a location originally intended for DevTools wiring, and the host would also be responsible for too much interpretation.

The position that stands is that host bindings connect to the checklist model, while the balance page connects to option construction and balance aggregation. Both paths can be triggered by the same integration, but each must be opened separately during review. Completed host wiring does not mean the filter options are correct; a filter menu with no duplicates does not mean that the checklist's returned results are stable enough for the host.

## Still undecided

- Whether Invalid Selection Fallback needs to pass the reason to the presentation layer has not been decided on this page;
- The type entry point still tends to be opened first; whether to add a more direct navigation note is left for the next related change;
- If the checklist continues to gain steps, "the page can render it" does not directly establish whether a stable order should be documented separately.

This version corrects the boundaries for investigation and responsibility; it does not invent field details that were not confirmed at the time.

# DevTools onboarding filtering and deduplication decision

This record was not organized into a single, start-to-finish explanation. What it preserves are the different issues caused by several Pay Card integrations: the earliest was whether DevTools onboarding could provide the host with a usable list; next was whether, after the balance Filter Option Merge and Deduplication, the displayed results could still be correctly understood; later, it was also discovered that old type entry points easily led investigators to mistake adjacent declarations for behavior definitions. All of these issues carried the Pay Card name, but they did not belong to the same implementation boundary.

Looking back now, the most valuable thing is not to rewrite all the old sections according to the current framing, but to preserve the scope of each judgment. Early on, the only understanding was that pages should not independently recalculate list progress; the interim review was what separated "the list has no duplicates" from "deduplication occurs in the correct place"; only later discussions separated the host's read relationship from the balance business rules. The old approach is still worth reading because it explains why someone would open the type declarations first, and why some notes appear to place the two changes in the same location.

## 2023-04: The two tracks in the initial record

When it was first registered, DevTools onboarding and Filter Option Merge and Deduplication were placed under the same integration item. There was a factual basis for writing it this way: both tasks needed to be reviewed when Pay Card entered the product entry point. But "the same integration round" is not "the same data flow." By then, two types of callers could already be distinguished: host tools needed to obtain the list for display and operation; the balance page needed a set of selectable filters and then used them to obtain balance results.

There were initially two candidates for the list portion.

The first candidate was to pass the step collection to the host as-is. When displaying it, the page would determine for itself which items were complete and refresh the values itself after the user switched an item; if multiple items needed to be changed at once, the page would traverse the collection. The advantage of this approach was that very little was exposed on the list side, and the page also appeared easy to integrate. Its problem was not that any particular page would necessarily fail, but that completion-status determination would be scattered across all host entry points. When steps were added later, one entry point might update its count while another still counted according to the old collection; both pages could render a list, but they might not show the same completion status.

The second candidate was to have the list model provide the results required for page display and modification. The host would no longer reinterpret whether each step was complete, but would read the content provided by the model to display progress and return user actions to the model for processing. This direction was provisionally selected. It did not require all Pay Card objects to use view models, nor did it turn the component layout into an interface; the decision applied only to the usage within DevTools that needed to display and modify the list.

At the time, the filter option was merely a short side note: "Remove duplicates after merging." This wording later led to a misreading. Some people interpreted "merge" to mean that the balance should also be normalized first, as if the option set and the filtered balance could be produced by the same piece of logic. The original meaning was narrower: options are the scope that users see and select, while the balance is the result calculated after a selection has been fixed. Options can be organized, but the balance must still retain its own state and priority assessment.

The first version left three boundaries that still explain why they were not combined at the time: list presentation should not depend on the host doing its own counting; option deduplication should not also perform balance calculation; and host wiring and balance-page logic must not be treated as the same place to make a change merely because they both appear in Pay Card. At that time, no fixed field list had been saved, nor was there a record of which key should be used to compare all duplicate items, so the old draft did not settle the details.

## The Appeal of the Early Type Entry Point

Early investigations generally started with `domain/entity/pay-card/src/types.ts`. This was not without reason. Near the type declaration, the adjacent definition of the Pay Card object was visible, and the file header also contained `import type { z } from "zod";`; to someone who had just taken over, it looked like a general entry point broad enough to house the list, filters, and balance.

At one point, a simple conclusion took shape: since the relevant objects could be found near the type layer, we should work out there, in one place, what the page needs to consume, and then let different entry points connect through the same declaration. This conclusion did not immediately reveal its problem, because it conflated "what can be found here" with "what should be decided here." The type layer mainly provides adjacency clues; that does not mean it owns the completion-status rules for the host's list, nor does it own the construction order of the filter options.

The type entry point is still worth keeping. When encountering old links or records that contain only the term Pay Card, starting from it can help locate neighboring objects. The change is in the purpose of reading it: it is a starting point for further navigation, not an all-in-one definition that can independently explain list returns and filtering behavior. This distinction later changed the investigation path and prevented a type adjustment from being mistaken for a change in the host's results.

## Review Addendum: Do Not Turn the Page into a Second Model

The first-round review did not reject the direction of the list model, but added a marginal note: host wiring cannot be described as part of the list definition. The host needs to obtain the list result and may also read tool controls at the same time; it therefore owns the read relationship, not the step-completion rules.

This marginal note targeted a common convenience pattern. Once a page has the steps, it is easy to calculate the completed count as a side effect; when batch changes are needed, it is also easy to iterate over and modify them in the page. Writing it this way in a single page does not seem complex, but once there is a second entry point, completion status, batch actions, and handling of new steps can each grow into a different version. The list model exists precisely so that every host does not have to reinterpret these behaviors.

The filter options have a corresponding boundary. The presentation layer can consume constructed options, and the balance page can pass valid selections to balance aggregation; but the presentation component should not deduplicate on the fly. If the page filters duplicate values itself, the list will look shorter on the surface, but the construction order will lose a traceable position. Invalid Selection Fallback, the display of selected items, and balance results would then have to be understood in terms of the page's secondary processing rather than in terms of option construction.

The review did not provide any universally applicable deduplication rule at the time. Not all input sets were retained, and no case was retained from which all comparison keys could be derived. The record therefore confirms only where responsibility lies: merging and deduplication belong to filter option construction; balance aggregation operates on an already determined filter scope; host wiring does not interpret options on behalf of the balance page. Mixing these responsibilities may seem to reduce the number of files, but in practice, when a problem occurs, it makes it impossible to tell whether the discrepancy was caused by input, construction, presentation, or aggregation.

## Retained Previous Approach (Deprecated)

The following passage has not been deleted from the historical record. It was once a seriously considered approach, but it later ceased to be applicable:

> Start by placing both the checklist and filtering near the Pay Card type declarations, and define the page's required return data in one place. The host, balance page, and option list integrate through the same object, which can reduce the number of searches across directories for the implementation.

The advantage of this approach was that it had few entry points. For someone who had only seen `domain/entity/pay-card/src/types.ts`, a unified entry point was also intuitive: the checklist, stablecoin balances, and filter options all sit alongside Pay Card, so it seemed they should first be organized next to the same declaration.

Its drawbacks only became clear later. The checklist is consumed by the host tool, which is concerned with display and modification; the options are consumed by the balance page, which is concerned with the selectable scope; aggregation logic operates on the already selected scope and the balance state. Even if all these objects can be reached by navigating from near a single type name, that does not imply that they are governed by a single return contract. The old approach treated navigational convenience as ownership of behavior, so it was not pursued further.

This passage is retained not to encourage later readers to choose it again, but to explain why some older troubleshooting records first point to the type layer. The old entry point is not a misleading clue; it simply cannot establish the current conclusion on its own. After reading it, proceed to the checklist model, option construction, or balance aggregation according to the object involved in the issue, rather than adding all behavior next to the type declarations.

## 2023-07: A Recheck Changed the Inspection Approach

Subsequent hands-on verification undermined two conclusions that things "already seemed to be working correctly".

First, the fact that the page can already display the checklist does not mean the host has obtained a stable checklist result. It may have received only a collection of steps, with progress still calculated on the fly by the page, and single-item actions and bulk actions may also be expanded separately on the page side. A visible checklist is not enough to confirm that the return boundary is properly enforced.

Second, the fact that the option list appears to have no duplicates does not mean deduplication occurs during construction. The presentation layer can also produce a menu without duplicate items by excluding identical options on the fly; but this approach does not explain the construction order, much less where Invalid Selection Fallback should be handled. If the balance results later differ from the user's expectations, the person troubleshooting cannot determine whether the discrepancy came from option inputs, presentation-layer processing, or aggregation processing.

After the recheck, the checklist-side checkpoint changed from "whether the checklist appears" to "whether the host relies solely on the results provided by the checklist model to perform rendering and modifications". If the host still reads private step details, calculates counts separately, or iterates through the collection itself to perform bulk modifications, the boundary has not truly been enforced. The focus here is on object responsibilities, not on which layout or components the page uses.

The checkpoint on the filtering side changed from "have the duplicates disappeared" to "does option construction preserve an explainable merge order". Deduplication may change the visible ordering; changes in ordering will in turn affect how consumers understand the current selection. Balance aggregation should only receive the finalized filter scope and continue calculating the filtered stablecoin balance. It should not handle duplicates on behalf of option construction, nor should it restore ordering for the presentation layer.

This review did not produce a new unified algorithm. The available material supports a decision about "where deduplication occurs", but is not sufficient to describe every type of input in terms of fixed comparison rules. The record therefore did not exaggerate any single visible result into universal behavior, retaining only the boundaries between construction, presentation, and aggregation.

## A Host-Side Proposal That Did Not Materialize

During the review, the host binding structure was proposed as a unified observation point. The rationale was that the host can see both the DevTools controls and the checklist results, so step state, option state, and page display information could seemingly all be brought together there. This would give callers just one entry point to open.

This proposal did not become the current decision. The binding layer is responsible for giving the host access to controls and checklist results, not recalculating checklist completion, much less stuffing filter-option deduplication and balance aggregation into tool properties. Putting balance business rules into the DevTools wiring would make the balance page depend on a location originally intended for host-side read relationships; putting checklist state back into the binding layer would also give both the model and the host their own ability to interpret steps.

The division retained was: host bindings connect to the checklist model; the balance page connects to option construction and balance aggregation. They can be triggered by the same integration and can also be modified within the same scheduling window, but a review of one cannot substitute for a review of the other. The host having read the results does not mean the filter menu is correct; the absence of duplicate filter options does not mean the host no longer needs to calculate checklist progress.

## A Short Excerpt from a Review Note

An internal review left two short reminders:

- "Don't make the page count steps."
- "Remove duplicates from the options first, don't make aggregation guess."

These two lines are not a complete design, nor are they a substitute for all implementation branches. They were retained because subsequent discussions repeatedly returned to the same boundary: the page does not take on the checklist model's calculations, and aggregation does not take on shaping the option list. Expanding these short lines into a set of unconfirmed rules would instead go beyond the judgments already reached at the time.

The same note also retained a reminder about the old entry point: do not remove the navigational value of the type layer, but after opening a type declaration, it should be possible to tell whether the next step is to look at the checklist, the options, or the balance. This reminder did not reject the earlier investigation path, but only corrected its endpoint. Type adjacency is a starting point, not where conclusions are reached.

## Diagram of the Observed Relationships

The diagram below shows only the reading relationships retained on this page, not that these objects are implemented in the same layer:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> TypeNeighbor
  TypeNeighbor: Type adjacency
  TypeNeighbor --> OnboardingModel
  TypeNeighbor --> FilterBuilder
  OnboardingModel: Checklist model
  FilterBuilder: Option construction
  OnboardingModel --> HostRendering
  HostRendering: Host rendering and editing
  FilterBuilder --> BalanceAggregation
  BalanceAggregation: Balance aggregation
```

The branch in the diagram was added later as a correction. The earliest version of the old proposal tended to aggregate everything all pages needed directly from type adjacency; after review, the type layer retains only a navigation role. The checklist model and option construction each address their own concerns, and balance aggregation takes place after the option scope has been determined. The diagram does not include the feature tour, quick actions, or additional card interface configuration, because although they are adjacent objects in Pay Card integration, they are not part of the two decisions on this page.

## Easily misinterpreted counterexamples

Counterexample one: A host page can render a list of steps, so this is taken to mean that the checklist interface is complete. This conclusion has already been overturned by a subsequent review. Being able to display a list only shows that the page has obtained some kind of step information; it does not show that completion status, individual edits, and bulk edits all belong to the same object. If the page still calculates progress itself, adding steps may create a risk of inconsistent counts across entry points.

Counterexample two: No duplicate options are visible in the filter menu, so balance filtering is assumed to be correct. This conclusion is also outdated. A menu that appears normal may simply mean that the presentation layer has temporarily filtered out duplicate items; it does not prove that option construction preserves the correct merge order, nor does it prove that no other discrepancies arose when the filter scope entered balance aggregation.

Counterexample three: Old troubleshooting records point to type declarations, so it is assumed that all related behavior should be determined at the type layer. This claim no longer applies either. The type entry point can still help locate objects around Pay Card, but the checklist model, option construction, and balance aggregation each have different responsibilities; being able to reach them from a directory does not mean that the directory defines them.

What these counterexamples have in common is not a requirement to run a comprehensive set of checks every time, but an effort to prevent three visible phenomena from replacing an assessment of the actual issue: seeing a checklist, seeing a menu without duplicates, and seeing type declarations cannot, on their own, prove that responsibilities are assigned to the right place.

## Adjacent issues not yet disentangled

The Invalid Selection Fallback of the filter options remains a related issue. The existing records show that fallback cannot be replaced by deduplication logic, but they do not preserve enough facts to determine whether the reason for fallback needs to be visible to the presentation layer. If users need to be notified in the future, confirm then whether the notification belongs to option construction, selection state, or the balance page; it must not be slipped into this decision under the label of "merging and deduplication".

Stable checklist ordering is another aspect that has not yet been disentangled. Checklist steps need to be displayed, toggled, and counted, but the early materials did not provide a complete ordering table that could serve as the sole source of truth. When adding steps in the future, check whether the additions also affect display, completion progress, and bulk changes; do not assume that statistics and operations need no adjustments just because a new item can be displayed.

One more reminder about scope. Feature tours, quick actions, and additional configuration for the card interface all come up in Pay Card integration discussions, and each also has its own visible states, actions, or session responsibilities. This page does not include these objects in the checklist's return shape, nor does it use the filter-option decision to infer their behavior. They are merely near the same product object, not extensions of this page's decision.

## Current requirements

Based on the records, reviews, earlier proposals, and rechecks above, the current requirements focus on the public boundary of the DevTools checklist model: the DevTools onboarding view model is located at devtools/pay-card/src/usePayCardViewModel.ts; its public return object retains the onboarding, steps, completedCount, totalCount, allDone, toggleStep, and setAllSteps fields, which callers use to display and modify the checklist.

This requirement replaces the old assumption that "it is enough for the page to receive the steps". Callers should display and modify the checklist based on the object returned by the model, rather than independently reconstructing completion progress or bulk operations. Checklist contents, completion progress, the total count, whether all items are complete, and action entry points are read from the same public result; the host retains responsibility for its own wiring and presentation, but no longer serves as a second place for checklist calculations.

The current requirements do not change the boundary on the filtering side. Merging and deduplication of filter options remain the responsibility of the logic that builds them, and balance aggregation still calculates the filtered stablecoin balance. The only thing the two sides have in common is that both were rechecked during Pay Card integration; appearing together does not mean they share an interface, and the checklist object cannot be used to endorse the filtering logic.

## Current order of investigation

If the issue manifests as the DevTools checklist not displaying correctly or not being modifiable as expected, first confirm that the host is reading the complete result returned by the checklist model, then check whether the caller is bypassing the model and performing its own calculations. Do not conclude that the return boundary is correct based solely on whether the page renders a few lines of text, and do not start by attributing the issue to changes in type declarations.

If the issue appears as duplicate filter menu items, an abnormal order or a balance that does not match expectations after a selection, first check option construction, then pass the already determined selection scope to balance aggregation for evaluation. Do not let the presentation layer's filtered results replace the decisions made during construction, and do not make balance aggregation responsible for deduplicating options. This lets you review the source of duplicates, the selection scope and the balance state separately.

`domain/entity/pay-card/src/types.ts` can still serve as a starting point for older records. When you encounter it, treat it as a navigation clue near the Pay Card declaration, rather than the overall definition of checklist and filtering behavior. This entry point is retained to support existing reading paths; it no longer carries this page's current decisions.

## Appendix of Old Examples

**Old Example One: The page only needs to display progress, so it can count completed steps on the fly from the steps array.**

This example was once used to support the "the raw collection is sufficient" approach. It no longer applies, because checklist presentation and checklist modification are now treated as part of the same return boundary. Counting on the fly in the page would shift the completion rules back to the caller, and adding steps would again introduce differences between entry points.

**Old Example Two: If the filter menu has no duplicate items, the balance filtering logic can be considered correct.**

This example is also outdated. The menu results show only one aspect of the displayed collection, not where deduplication occurs, much less how balance aggregation handles the filter scope. It is retained so that anyone who encounters old screenshots or notes knows that what was overlooked at the time was the distinction between where construction happens and the calculations that follow.

**Old Example Three: Related objects can be reached from the type declarations, so the type layer is the only entry point for review.**

This example is retained as a historical reading aid. It explains why early investigations focused on a single directory, but it can no longer serve as a basis for assessing the current implementation. The type layer can lead to adjacent objects; checklists, options and balances still need to be verified at their respective objects.

## Notes for the Next Change

The next time work involves adding checklist steps, changing host bindings or regression testing filter options, there is no need to rewrite this history. Simply follow the object involved in the issue to the relevant location: for checklist changes, check whether the return boundary still supports presentation and modification; for filter changes, check whether merging and deduplication still take place during option construction; for balance anomalies, check the state after the determined filter scope enters aggregation. The old approaches, entry points and examples remain to explain existing reading paths, but no longer serve as the basis for the current implementation.

# Host binding pricing proposal

This is an interface draft, starting by clarifying what the host tools need to receive. To follow the earlier investigation notes, continue from the issue entry point `useFeatureFlagsToolProps.ts`; the direct dependencies found include `useMemo`, Redux selectors, and the feature flag hook. The question here isn't about creating a second set of Pay Card state, but deciding whether the binding layer should return raw flags or prepared tool properties.

There are two options:

- The binding layer gives the host only the current flags and an entry point for updating them, leaving Filter Option Display Pricing for the balance page to handle.
- The binding layer also prepares the filter options and their display values, so the host consumes a single result.

The second option is easier to integrate, but it would put balance display rules into the host bindings. When filter options change later, the changes could easily end up half on one side and half on the other. We're leaning toward the first option for now: keep the binding layer thin, with the host depending only on stable fields. We still need to confirm the actual export shape and whether onboarding belongs in this layer's long-term interface.

TODO: Check against the current binding implementation to confirm the flag field names, write actions, and ownership of Filter Option Display Pricing. If the host still needs to modify Pay Tab directly, this proposal must be withdrawn if it would allow the host to bypass the existing feature flag write path.

# Host Binding Pricing Proposal

The previous version kept "Filter Option Display Pricing" outside the binding layer because the visible dependencies were mainly around feature flags; that still stands. After review, the proposal needs a tighter scope: the host needs tool properties that let it read flags, trigger changes, and get tour-related data, not another implementation of balance aggregation.

The old entry point is still listed as `devtools/bindings/src/useFeatureFlagsToolProps.ts`. It now looks more like a pointer left over from an earlier investigation and cannot directly determine the public interface. If the binding layer only returns the raw override, the host will assemble its own set of fields; if it returns too much page state, the responsibilities for filter-option pricing and the balance page will get mixed together again.

So the proposal is now "the binding layer provides stable controls; display calculations stay with the consumer." The proposed return shape is below; field names still need to be checked against the implementation:

- Current feature flag values and actions to change them;
- The onboarding state needed by the Pay Card tool;
- No filtered balances or pricing text as fixed fields in the binding layer.

This sacrifices some convenience on the host side, but keeps the binding layer from growing further to meet a single page's display needs. If the code already includes filter options in the binding output, the second approach can still be kept, but we first need to confirm that it uses the same state rather than performing another merge in the host.

The main Card-side check is whether the filter text users see after the command completes still matches the balance page; this page alone cannot determine that implementation outcome. We'll leave the interface boundary here and wait to rename or remove fields until the exports and caller shapes along the current path are confirmed.

Open questions: whether the host must modify Pay Tab directly; whether onboarding is a complete object or just an entry point for reading tour steps; which side owns the final formatting rules for Filter Option Display Pricing. The conditions for withdrawing the proposal remain the emergence of two writable copies of feature flag state, or the host duplicating balance aggregation logic to display pricing.

# Host Binding and Valuation Proposal

### Assumptions Revised in This Round

The early draft put the host binding and Filter Option Display Pricing in the same interface diagram, then treated the former as a thin wrapper around "read-only flags." A recent review of the binding files and their consumption patterns showed that the second assessment wasn't accurate either: the host doesn't just read the current value. It needs to pass the controls already available on the tool side to the Pay Card tool, while allowing page onboarding to be consumed through the same set of props.

The entry point in the old notes was `devtools/bindings/src/useFeatureFlagsToolProps.ts`. The binding module to check now is `devtools/bindings/src/usePayCardToolProps.ts`. These names are not interchangeable: the former only shows that the earlier investigation started with a feature flags issue; the latter is the public entry point for verifying the Pay Card tool's props in this round.

### Current Interface Shape

The host binding is provided by devtools/bindings/src/usePayCardToolProps.ts; it keeps payTabEnabled and setCardParam as the public flags and passes the same onboarding contract to the Pay Card tool.

"Keep" has two practical meanings here. `payTabEnabled` is the flag value read by the host, and `setCardParam` is the entry point used to modify the card configuration. They should not be replaced with another set of temporary fields just because the DevTools page adds onboarding. Nor does `onboarding` mean copying every page's display copy into the binding layer; it lets the tool read the existing onboarding state and step-control shape. The binding layer can use memo to assemble the returned object, but it must not use this as an opportunity to move balance-filtering calculations into this layer.

The adjacent dependencies visible in the file are still:

- `useMemo` handles stable composition of the binding results;
- `useDispatch` and `useSelector` connect to Redux state;
- `setOverride`, `setAllOverrides`, and `featureFlagsOverridesSelector` correspond to flag reads and writes;
- `useFeatureFlags` provides the read entry point on the platform feature flag side.

These dependencies support a shape in which the host reads and modifies controls, but they do not support claiming that filtered stablecoin balances or valuation text are outputs of the binding layer. Filter Option Display Pricing still needs to be checked in the balance feature's own consumption path. Forcing it into this layer would make the binding interface responsible for both state writes and page formatting, leaving us unable to tell later whether the host parameters were wrong or the display side recalculated the value.

### Two Consumer Scenarios

The DevTools scenario needs to use the controls returned by the binding to change the Pay Tab state, then check whether onboarding in the tool still follows the original contract. The concerns here are whether the fields remain stable and whether updates still go through the same feature flag state. The binding layer does not need to know how prices are displayed for every filter option.

The balance page scenario works the other way around: it needs to derive filter options from its own balance state, then aggregate the filtered results into the valuation shown on the page. The host can provide control flags, but it should not decide how the balance page merges, deduplicates, or formats its filter options. The available material does not identify an implementation entry point for this part, so this proposal does not describe it as a completed interface.

### Trade-offs Left After Review

We considered having the binding layer return an "all-in-one" Pay Card view model, with the host only forwarding it. That would remove one piece of wiring, but it would couple cross-platform page state with DevTools control state; any balance display change could become a host interface change. We also considered continuing to use `useFeatureFlagsToolProps.ts` and simply appending Pay Card fields to its return value. This would appear compatible to existing callers, but the filename and responsibilities would no longer explain where onboarding comes from, and investigations would continue to conflate feature flags with the Pay Card tool.

The decision is therefore to keep a dedicated Pay Card binding entry point, expose stable flags and card-parameter actions, pass through the agreed onboarding contract, and not generate Filter Option Display Pricing here. If implementation checks find that host code already depends on reading the old hook directly, reassess compatibility forwarding. Until then, do not delete the old path or treat it as evidence for the new interface.

### Withdrawal Criteria

If any of the following occurs, the proposal must go back for review:

1. `setCardParam` does not actually modify the card parameters the host is using, leaving the page and tool with separate state after DevTools changes a value;
2. The binding layer and consumer maintain onboarding steps separately and cannot share the same completion state;
3. To obtain Filter Option Display Pricing, the binding layer has to duplicate the balance aggregation logic;
4. Existing callers can only accept the full return shape of `useFeatureFlagsToolProps.ts` and cannot read the new Pay Card props through compatibility forwarding.

These conditions have not all been verified in the actual environment. At the next check, inspect the current hook's exported object and a real caller first, then decide whether a compatibility layer is needed; do not start by inferring the binding interface from the displayed result.

# DevTools Controls and Navigation Troubleshooting Tree

Start by splitting the issues by where they appear. "Pay Card has no entry point" could mean the tool control in the host, or the navigation in PayTab. Don't combine these two symptoms yet; one is whether the host can display the control, and the other is whether the screen has reached the navigation check.

```
Entry points don't match
├─ No control in DevTools
│  └─ First ask whether the host has a Pay Card item
└─ No navigation in PayTab
   └─ First confirm whether the screen is still showing login content
```

The initial working assumption was that the control and navigation shared a single card toggle, and changing the toggle would return the page to the correct state. This assumption gave the investigation a starting point at the time; there weren't enough counterexamples yet.

On the page side, start with `apps/ledger-live-mobile/src/mvvm/features/PayTab/screens/PayTab/PayTabView.tsx` for now. Here you can see `React`, `CardLogin`, the type `OpenHostedLogin`, and `Box`. `CardLogin` can only help assess whether the screen may still be login-adjacent; it doesn't tell us whether the host has already provided the control.

If the repro comes from DevTools, stay on the tool side first; don't infer whether the control is bound from the PayTab page. If the person reporting the repro only says "I didn't see the navigation" but provides neither the current screen nor the entry point location, don't label it as a state anomaly yet.

Keep the old sequence in place for the time being: open PayTab and confirm whether it's still showing login content; then check the toggle in the tool; finally return to the page. This only fits the single-page issue from that time; we still need to establish whether the control and navigation really share state.

# DevTools Controls and Tour Troubleshooting Tree

"There's no entry point for Pay Card" still comes up in field reports. That statement cannot be taken as a conclusion. It could mean that the DevTools control isn't showing in the host, or that PayTab is already open but the feature tour isn't showing; another possibility is that the control is present, but the page stays on the same content after it is used. All three descriptions have been called toggle issues in older records.

```
"No entry point" reported
|
+-- Looking for the control in the DevTools interface
|   |
|   +-- No Pay Card item
|   |   `-- Stay on the host-tool side
|   |
|   `-- Control is present, but the screen doesn't change after use
|       `-- First record which screen is still showing
|
`-- Looking for the tour in PayTab
    |
    +-- Still on login-related content
    |   `-- Not yet at the point of assessing the tour
    |
    `-- Target screen reached, but no tour visible
        `-- Check visibility state separately
```

## Guidance Left Over from the First Draft

The earliest approach treated the card toggle as a shared gate: if the tool had the control, the page should be reachable; if the page was reachable, the tour should appear too. This gave troubleshooting a single starting action, but lumped three different things into one statement.

There was a practical reason to look at `apps/ledger-live-mobile/src/mvvm/features/PayTab/screens/PayTab/PayTabView.tsx` first at the time. `CardLogin` was near that page, and the most common screens encountered in the field were still showing login-related content. The page entry point is useful for that assessment, but that doesn't make it the starting point for every Pay Card symptom.

The old rule is retained verbatim:

> Change the card toggle first, then refresh PayTab; as long as the screen appears, the tour will come back too.

This rule can now only be used to interpret the old records. It doesn't answer whether the host has received the control, nor, when a user can't see the tour on the target screen, whether the missing piece is reaching the screen, evaluating visibility, or a previously handled state.

## A Page Review

During the page review, the only directly visible adjacent references were `React`, `CardLogin`, the type `OpenHostedLogin`, and `Box`. These imports were enough to separate "still on login content" and "tour not shown" into two questions: for the former, first confirm whether the page has reached the target location; only the latter calls for further investigation of the tour.

You can't infer the form of the host tool's controls from these imports. Nor can every action that has no effect be attributed to login just because `CardLogin` is nearby. Whether the page remains on login content is an observation that can be recorded; whether the host provides a control is a different question.

One unsuccessful investigation started right here. Someone saw that an action in the tool didn't produce the expected screen change and started tracing down through the page components. The page could show what content was on screen, but provided no evidence of whether the control had been bound. The investigation ended with only a page entry point, not a reusable set of fix steps.

Another mistaken assessment treated "the user has seen the tour before" and "there is no tour now" as the same thing. A later review separated them: the former describes a historical state, while the latter describes the screen now. Not seeing the tour now doesn't automatically mean it was closed, nor does prior handling of the tour automatically mean there are no other conditions for reaching the page.

## Actions by Branch

When a reproduction comes in, establish two facts first: whether the person reproducing it is looking at DevTools or PayTab, and whether login content is still occupying the page. Without those two facts, do not proceed on the claim that "the tour is broken."

If there is no control in DevTools, record it as missing at the control layer and stop at the host tool's binding boundary. Don't require the page side to prove that it's working first, and don't record a missing control as a closed tour.

If the control is present but the screen still shows login-related content after use, record the screen first. `CardLogin` can remain an adjacent reference here, but the only conclusion is that we haven't confirmed reaching the point where the tour is assessed.

If the target screen has been reached but the tour isn't visible, move on to the tour's visibility state and recovery actions. The page path is still useful here, but it cannot replace checking the state.

## Review Addendum

The review required separate documentation of the control entry point, adjacent login references, and tour visibility. This wasn't to add troubleshooting steps, but to prevent one page screenshot from being treated as evidence for tool binding, reaching the screen, and state restoration all at once.

Symptoms recorded from then on should fall into a precise branch: no control appears in DevTools; PayTab is still on login content; or no tour is visible on the target screen. These can occur together or be unrelated. If even the location in the interface can't be confirmed, stop because the reproduction description is insufficient; don't draw a conclusion about the tour state.

## Old Step Retained

"Open PayTab first" has not been removed. For someone with only the mobile page available, it can still help confirm whether `CardLogin` occupies the current path. If it's already clear that the screen is on login content, address the conditions for reaching the screen first; don't describe a page symptom as the tour being closed.

However, this old step doesn't apply to reports where the host has no control at all, or where differences in control display across platforms haven't yet been explained. Continuing to start with the page will only make it the default place issues get assigned.

One related question remains open: whether host tools on different platforms provide controls in exactly the same form. The existing records aren't enough to attribute layout differences, input row differences, or binding differences to the same cause, so leave this out of the tree for now.

# DevTools Control and Tour Troubleshooting Tree

"The Pay Card entry point is gone" is still an insufficient problem description. Older records called the host DevTools control, the current PayTab screen and the feature tour entry points, causing control-layer issues to be routed to the page, and failures to reach the page to be recorded as the tour state not having been restored. Before troubleshooting, first ask the person reproducing the issue to point out the interface they are looking at.

The old page-side navigation is still in `apps/ledger-live-mobile/src/mvvm/features/PayTab/screens/PayTab/PayTabView.tsx`. There you can see `React`,`CardLogin`, and the types `OpenHostedLogin` and `Box`. This shows that login content is a related area to check when troubleshooting the page, but does not prove that the DevTools control has appeared, nor can it explain on its own whether the tour is visible.

The latest triage flow starts with symptoms, not with a particular page file:

```text
The person reproducing the issue says "there is no entry point"
|
+-- Points to the DevTools interface
|   |
|   +-- No Pay Card control
|   |   `-- Stop at host binding and the control layer
|   |
|   `-- The control is present, but the screen does not change after interaction
|       `-- Record the interaction target and current screen, then branch to login or tour troubleshooting
|
`-- Points to the PayTab screen
    |
    +-- Still showing login-related content
    |   `-- The tour check has not yet been reached
    |
    `-- The target screen has been reached, but no feature tour is visible
        `-- Check visibility state, viewed state and the close action
```

This is not a long process that must be completed every time. It only requires each step to answer a question about one object. Stop at the point where there is no local object to check further, and record the stopping point as "control did not appear", "still on login content" or "no tour visible on the target screen". Do not combine these different symptoms into "Pay Card is unavailable".

## 2023-03-20: Initial Page Notes

The first version started with PayTabView because the screen being viewed at the time was a mobile screen.`CardLogin` appeared in the adjacent imports, so the natural first question on the spot was whether the page had moved away from the login content. That note treated the tool control and the tour as two outcomes of the same card toggle: when the toggle was on, the page would appear, and the tour should also appear.

At the time, the sequence was short: open PayTab; if it was still showing login content, first inspect the login-related screen; then toggle the card switch once in the tool; finally return to the page and look for the walkthrough. This sequence was not entirely useless for a reproduction consisting only of a page screenshot, but it did not make clear who provided the control, nor did it distinguish between no walkthrough currently being shown and a walkthrough having been handled in the past.

The initial draft retained the following assessment:

> The control and the walkthrough share one switch; once the switch is changed correctly, the page will return to the correct state on its own.

That statement was later disproven, but it was not deleted. Old on-call records repeatedly used it as a premise, so it explains why early troubleshooting began with the page, and also why "control missing" and "walkthrough not displayed" were once written in the same paragraph.

The initial notes did not contain enough material to explain how the host tool supplied controls on different platforms. Nor was there evidence showing what determined whether the walkthrough was displayed on screen. At that time, the only thing that could be confirmed was that the page contained a login-related adjacent element; the reproducer would mix it up with the walkthrough issue in reports.

## A Note Added in the Margin of the Old Page

Later, during on-call, someone followed the old sequence and opened PayTab, only to find that the controls in the tool did not appear at all. Continuing to inspect the page could answer only whether it was still showing login content, not why the host had not provided the control. The note left in the old page's margin was: check the reproduction location first; do not look at the page first.

This marginal note did not change the page implementation or provide a new binding conclusion on the spot. It only narrowed the way the question was asked: first ask whether the issue occurred in DevTools or PayTab; if it occurred in PayTab, then ask whether the screen was still occupied by login content. If any one of these is missing, do not rush to investigate the walkthrough state.

After this margin note, records no longer treated "the entry is gone" as a final conclusion. It could only serve as a symptom heading; the details below had to be tied to a specific interface. That way, when reviewing later, it would at least be possible to distinguish whether an old record was about the host control or the walkthrough on the page.

## A Page Trace That Did Not Work

On one review, both phenomena were traced together through the page components: the tool had no control, and the tool had a control but the screen did not change after the operation. Because `CardLogin` was a visible adjacent element, the initial guess was that the login condition was blocking the subsequent content.

This guess covered only some of the possibilities. When the control was already present and the screen was still showing login content, it was worth continuing to investigate the page's reachability conditions; when the control had not appeared at all, whether the page displayed login content could not tell anyone whether binding had occurred. The two phenomena were not separated at the time, and the trace left no reusable remediation steps.

"The screen does not change after the operation" also had two meanings. One was that the operation had not reached the page; the other was that the page had already reached the target location but the walkthrough was not displayed. For the former, the control and the operation target first had to be retained; only the latter required entering the walkthrough branch. The old trace directly recorded the gap in between as a switch failure, so it answered neither of these boundary questions.

This failed record remains here. It is not meant to say that the page entry has no value; it is a reminder to later readers: an adjacent import can help identify the current screen, but it cannot prove binding for the host tool, nor can it provide an answer about the walkthrough state.

## 2023-11-27: Narrowed scope after review

The page review confirmed only local adjacency: `apps/ledger-live-mobile/src/mvvm/features/PayTab/screens/PayTab/PayTabView.tsx` imports `React`, `CardLogin`, the type `OpenHostedLogin`, and `Box`. On this basis, "still showing login content" and "the tour is not showing" can be investigated as two separate steps.

The review did not establish PayTabView as the location of the implementation of DevTools. Page files can serve as screen-side entry points, but not as the default route into the control layer. In particular, when the person reproducing the issue explicitly refers to the DevTools window, tracing downward from the page will only lead the investigation back to the wrong side.

That revision changed the minimum information recorded in the field to two items: the UI location and the current screen state. For the UI location, record only DevTools or PayTab; for the current screen state, record only still showing login content, already on the target screen, or not yet confirmed. Reports that "the entry point is gone" without this information remain incomplete descriptions.

For PayTab, `CardLogin` is treated as a screen-level adjacency, not as a synonym for the tour being closed. If the screenshot or reproduction notes show that login content is still displayed, the conclusion is that the tour cannot yet be assessed; only if the target screen has already been reached should the next question be whether the tour appears. This sequence reduced cases where the conditions for reaching a page were incorrectly described as state restoration problems.

For DevTools, whether the control exists should first be addressed within the scope of the host tool and the control layer. It is not up to the page layer to prove that the control should appear. When the control exists but an action does not produce the expected result, do not immediately call it a tour malfunction either; first record where the screen ends up after the action.

## Boundaries retained after review

The feedback retained from the review was: stop using "the toggle is not working" to summarize the entire set of symptoms. This wording conflates at least three things: whether the host has a control, whether PayTab has moved away from login content, and whether the feature tour is visible. They may be related, but the available material does not justify describing that relationship as a fixed causal link.

The recording format subsequently adopted was straightforward: object name first, symptom second. For example, "No Pay Card control appears in DevTools", "PayTab is still showing login-related content", "The target screen has been reached, but no tour is visible". Each of these three statements can be true independently; they do not need to occur together, nor does the same person reproducing the issue have to answer all three in one go.

The review also added a stopping condition: if the UI location cannot be confirmed, do not hand the issue off to the tour state. Without a UI location, "the tour is broken" is only a secondhand report. At this point, continuing to investigate the page path, dismissal action, or restored state could record an unknown as a negative.

The old rule "first change the toggle, then refresh PayTab" was marked as deprecated after this review. It can still help explain historical screenshots and old on-call logbooks, but it must not be used as the first action for current cross-platform control issues. In particular, when the host control does not exist, refreshing the page will not supply an entry point that is already missing.

## Limited steps still in use

"First open PayTab" still has one limited use: when only a mobile screenshot is available, first check whether the screenshot still shows login-related content. If so, record that the page has not yet reached the point where the tour is evaluated, and do not expect the tour state to explain it; if not, the old procedure ends here, and investigation moves on to the visible issue with the tour.

This step does not apply to reports where the control does not appear in DevTools. Nor does it apply to reports where all that is known is that one platform differs, but it is not yet known whether the difference is in the layout, the input row, or the host binding. Treating the page as the default entry point will obscure the gap at the control layer.

Therefore, the label "page first, only for page symptoms" is retained next to the old step. Keeping it does not endorse the old shared-toggle assessment, but allows records left along the old path to remain readable. When using it, the first question is still which part of the UI the person reproducing the issue is looking at.

## Discuss tour issues separately

The tour not being displayed, being dismissed by the user, having been viewed before, and state restoration are different descriptions of the situation. Early materials lumped them together as the tour disappearing, and they were later separated. The tour not being visible now does not automatically mean a dismissal occurred; a previous dismissal does not automatically mean the current page has no other display conditions.

When the only thing that can be confirmed on site is "there is no tour on the target screen", record only the current visibility. Do not add a user action. If a dismissal can be confirmed, keep the dismissal action and event context in the record, then ask whether the state is as expected. If it cannot even be confirmed whether the target screen has been reached, first return to the screen branch.

When state restoration is raised, the conditions for reaching the screen must not be skipped either. A restoration description concerns how historical state is retrieved for reuse, while current visibility concerns whether the screen should display the tour at this moment. The two are related, but they are not things that a single page observation can confirm at the same time.

The minimal tree for the tour branch is as follows:

```text
Confirmed that the target screen has been reached
|
+-- Cannot confirm the current tour assessment
|   `-- Stop at the visible model and fill in the current state
|
+-- Not displayed, and no information about a dismissal action
|   `-- Distinguish between the previously viewed state and the restoration boundary
|
`-- A dismissal action can be confirmed
    `-- Record the action context, then check the resulting state
```

This tree deliberately leaves out control toggles. Control issues are handled in the earlier triage; once in the tour branch, the issue is already about the relationship between the current state and actions. If it is later discovered that the control never appeared at all, return to the control layer rather than guessing at intermediate causes within the tour branch.

## Old questions about platform differences

In old records, someone described adjacent issues as "Web and native toggles are different". This statement did not preserve enough information: the difference could come from the section layout, the native input row, or the host binding. The old statement can no longer be treated as a conclusion.

The available material confirms that cross-platform controls need to be located through different entry points; it does not support claiming that every host tool provides controls in exactly the same form. For reports that occur on only one platform, retain the platform information and reproduction location, and do not automatically attribute the differences to the page or tour state.

Another issue that has not been split out is the precise scope of tour state restoration. The existing records are sufficient to distinguish viewed status from current visibility, but the complete caller-side materials were not retained to explain every point at which restoration occurs. This issue remains open; for now, record the entry point and current screen where the issue occurs, without guessing to fill in the restoration rules.

## Revisions after the old meeting excerpt

During the meeting review, someone raised the question: since `CardLogin` can be seen in the page path, could all cases of "not showing" be routed to login checks first. The conclusion was no. `CardLogin` can only help identify that the page is still adjacent to login; it does not mean that the tool controls already exist, nor that the tour on the target screen has been closed.

Another rejected practice was to jump directly from "no change after operating the control" to "the switch did not take effect". This wording skips whether the operation reached the page, whether the page reached the target location, and whether the tour was displayed. We now retain "screen unchanged after the action" as an intermediate record until the next fact is available.

After the meeting, the old paragraphs were not all rewritten. The original shared-switch claim, page-first steps, and failure tracing were all left in the preceding text, with only their scope of applicability and the locations of subsequent revisions marked alongside them. This lets people reviewing the old investigation understand why it took that direction at the time, without mistaking the old method for the current conclusion.

## Current control-layer entry points

When reproduction clearly occurs at the DevTools control layer, no longer work backward from PayTabView. The fixed navigation entry points for DevTools cross-platform controls are devtools/pay-card/src/components/Section/Section.web.tsx and devtools/pay-card/src/components/ToggleRow/ToggleRow.native.tsx, with the Web Section container continuing to use flex flex-col gap-12.

These two entry points are used to examine Web section rendering separately from native toggleable configuration rows. When the section layout is abnormal on the Web, start with Section; when a native configuration row cannot be toggled as expected, start with ToggleRow. Both can broadly be called controls, but the same page path should not be expected to explain both sides.

The current navigation only addresses where to start investigating. Whether the host passes controls to the corresponding interface still needs to be confirmed at the binding boundary; whether the page has left the login content is still confirmed by the actual screen of PayTab; whether the tour is displayed continues to be answered by the tour's visibility and state outputs. The three paths being adjacent does not mean they are interchangeable.

When the control is already present but the action has no effect, the next question is still which screen is currently displayed. If the screen is still showing login-related content, record that the page-arrival condition is unconfirmed; do not record that the tour has been closed. If it is already the target screen, proceed to the tour tree and separately record whether it is displayed, whether a viewed state is present, and whether a close action exists.

## Outdated quick-fix procedure

The following is the original procedure from the old on-call log. It is retained, but is no longer the preferred approach:

1. Start inspecting the page from PayTabView;
2. After finding login-related content, assume that the tour is controlled by the same switch;
3. Toggle the switch once in the tool;
4. Return to the page to check the tour.

The problem is in the second step. The presence of `CardLogin` on the page can only suggest that the current screen may not have left the login-adjacent area. It does not prove that the control and the tour share the same state, much less that the host has already exposed the control to the UI. The old procedure is suitable for interpreting historical records, not for the initial assessment of missing cross-platform controls.

The old appendix also treated "the control appears" as a sufficient condition for "the tour will appear". Subsequent counterexamples have disproved this assessment: the control's presence, arrival at the page, and tour visibility should be confirmed separately. The current branching is not intended to add extra steps, but to prevent an observation about one object from being used to draw a conclusion about another.

## What to leave for the next review

At the end of troubleshooting, leave only the branch actually followed and the stopping point. For example: the control did not appear, and investigation stopped at host binding; the page is still showing login content, and tour assessment has not yet begun; or the target screen has been reached, and the tour's visibility state remains to be checked. Records like these let the next person continue investigating without expanding a single local observation into a conclusion about the entire chain.

The shape of the cross-platform host's controls is still unconfirmed, and the caller boundary for restoring the tour state is also still unconfirmed. Neither should be treated as answered based on page screenshots or a single toggle operation. If new material becomes available, add it to the corresponding branch first, then decide whether a separate record needs to be split out.

The initial draft treated the view model in DevToolsScreen as the main destination for the tour migration. That assessment remains in the record: the earlier investigation did land in that file first, but this only shows that the issue name and the call name meet at the screen layer. A correct label only shows that the step was read as the expected text; the tour no longer appearing, or reappearing after a restore, is the result of a different state path.

The initial draft compared three approaches. The first was to replace the stable step ID directly with the visible title. This would require the fewest UI changes, but callers, completion calculations, and existing selection state would also lose the original key. The second was to adjust the display text after reading the steps, leaving ID for state and callers. The third was to move formatting and slice changes forward together, hoping to remove both sets of old logic at once.

At the time, the second display approach was adopted, and the third was not approved to proceed. This decision has a narrow scope: display text should not change step keys as a side effect. The earlier claim that "the slice can be moved once the display format is confirmed" was later overturned; getting the correct text through one display path does not prove that state was marked after closing, or that the restore entry point read the same state.

On mobile, `apps/ledger-live-mobile/src/mvvm/features/DevTools/screens/DevToolsScreen/useDevToolsScreenViewModel.ts` can still serve as an early lead. The file shows `useMemo`, `useSafeAreaInsets`, `NativeStackNavigationOptions`, and `useTheme` adjacent to one another. They explain why the investigation first stopped at the screen layer, but are not enough to conclude that the slice should be persisted as part of the screen lifecycle. That ownership assessment no longer applies.

During the review, the items that needed separate checks were drawn as the two chains below. The diagram is not a runtime state diagram; it shows the check order used at the time to avoid treating a display regression as a migration regression.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Stable step ID" as stable_id
  state "Visible label" as visible_label
  state "Viewed state" as viewed_state
  state "Mark operation" as marked
  state "Reset operation" as reset
  state "Restore entry point" as restored

  [*] --> stable_id
  stable_id --> visible_label: Read for display
  visible_label --> [*]

  [*] --> viewed_state
  viewed_state --> marked: Mark
  marked --> reset: Reset
  reset --> restored: Read on restore
  restored --> [*]
```

If a step name looks wrong, first check the conversion from stable ID to the visible label; do not start by changing the step key. If the tour reappears after being closed, or does not appear after a restore, check whether the sequence of marking, resetting, and reading on restore is still intact. If a change touches both sides, the regression record should separately state the label that was seen and whether the tour appeared; neither can stand in for the other.

CARD-206 is intended to add regression coverage in the repository for user-visible results, not to assert against internal helper function names. It supports separating display formatting from ID, but does not show that tour state has already been migrated. CARD-223 calls for running migration checks through public entry points and recording what is actually returned or thrown; it does not designate a single host either. The two cards retain their respective entry points for follow-up checks.

Another rejected approach was to attach tour state directly to the lifecycle of a single DevTools screen. This would make the entry path straightforward, but whether state was retained after leaving the screen would become a screen implementation detail. The review did not establish a new single home for the state; it only rejected the inference that the screen's location could be treated as the state boundary.

Placing the display conversion too early would leave multiple UIs maintaining their own text; placing it too late would require the UI to understand raw ID. No common location was specified for the conversion in this review; only the decision "do not change keys for display" was retained. If formatting is to be centralized later, we will still need to confirm which UIs actually share the same set of steps.

This record preserves the initial draft's choice regarding stable ID, as well as the corrected assessment of the migration entry point. It does not mean the migration is complete; at the time, we could settle the display boundary and decide that label changes, the location of a single screen file, or a single display regression should not be used as evidence that the tour migration was complete.
