title: Section and Quick Actions Migration Guide

versions.body:
# Section and Quick Actions Migration Guide

In this cumulative integration, Section's semantic markup and Quick Action Wrapper were handled together in a single compatibility migration. Both changes had passed page checks when they landed independently, but when integrators had only the registration information, the section's heading hierarchy and the shape of the action wrapper were not necessarily both preserved.

For the old entry point, start with `devtools/registry/src/types.ts`. Follow the migration order agreed at the time: first register Section's heading and child content as a single section object, then integrate quick actions as children of that section; don't replace the wrapper on the page first and come back to fill in the registration type. The latter approach temporarily leaves callers seeing only action names, with no way to tell which section they originally belonged to.

Keep the original section name during the migration; don't replace the semantic name with display text. If the presentation layer needs changes to spacing or heading styles, continue to get the heading and content from the section object; Quick Action Wrapper is only responsible for placing actions into an existing section, not for reinterpreting what the actions mean. This way, Web and non-Web entry points can at least build the page using the same registration information.

Check only two things during migration:

1. After a section with a heading and child content is registered, the heading still appears before the actions, and the wrapper has not swallowed the child content.
2. After a quick action under a section is clicked or hidden, the host can still recognize the section itself; do not replace the section object with a standalone array of actions.

The counterexample at the time was moving quick actions to the top level of the page first, then using display order to simulate sections. The page looked close to the original, but integrators could not tell whether an action belonged to Section; adding the heading back later would introduce a second wrapper. This backfill approach is not accepted here; directly restore the structure of "section registration first, actions as children."

If the heading is missing after migration, remove the new wrapper first, restore the old section object, then check whether the registration type can still represent the heading and child content. If the heading is fine but actions are missing, restore only the action children; don't change Section's name at the same time. Combining both kinds of recovery in one change will obscure whether the issue was in registration or wrapping.

Keep the previous responsibility split: the section registration side maintains Section's semantic markup; the page integration side decides whether quick actions need to be wrapped in that section. The registration side does not add special visual fields for individual actions, and the page side should not bypass registration to directly construct a section with the same name.

This record treats the two as a single compatibility issue for now. If a later integration changes only Section and does not require changes to Quick Action Wrapper, still follow the recovery order given here.

versions.body:
# ToggleRow and Cross-Platform Persistence Decision

This record was initially easy to read as an implementation task: add native input to ToggleRow, then make Pay Card state restore across platforms. After review, we retained this parallel relationship but no longer treat it as a single-track requirement. The two things will come together in the same manual regression, but they change how user input, state interpretation, and the host entry point are assessed.

The existing entry point is still `devtools/registry/src/types.ts`. It is the existing TypeScript module; the file header shows React's `ComponentType`, `LazyExoticComponent`, and zod. The initial draft viewed this as a possible convergence point because registry entries usually describe the label, component shape, and validation shape at the same time. That observation remains valid; directly inferring rendering or persistence responsibility for ToggleRow from it is not valid. The type table can help trace how an object is registered, but it cannot replace checking the native component and the location of state restoration.

## Judgment retained from the initial draft

The draft's working hypothesis was: if native input and cross-platform recovery appear in the same regression symptom, it is best to handle them together in one change. The apparent benefit of this idea is simplicity, with only one entry point; testers would not first have to explain whether a given toggle belonged to UI or was a state issue.

The counterexample raised during review was direct. Native ToggleRow is concerned with whether the input control captures the user's current toggle; Cross-Platform Pay Card Persistence is concerned with how existing state is interpreted on another platform or on the next entry. Even if the former is already usable, that does not automatically show that recovery has not overwritten it; even if the latter recovers consistently, that does not show that the native control actually presents toggleable input. Binding them to the same "success" conclusion would hide the location of the failure.

Therefore, the draft's merged approach was abandoned. The original paragraph is retained because it explains why subsequent records are not organized around a single feature toggle, not because it remains the recommended implementation approach.

## The three boundaries considered at the time

The first was centered on registry. The approach was to gather the native component, host entry point, and recovery rules around the types and registry entries. Its advantage is that names are centralized, so possible labels and component types can be found quickly while reading. The problem is equally clear: `devtools/registry/src/types.ts` provides only a local declaration and adjacent navigation. Forcing state recovery into this entry would make the registry layer carry behavioral meaning that it does not show.

The second was centered on the control. Native ToggleRow was treated as an independent object, with the focus on what boolean input it receives, how it triggers a toggle, and what the upper layer receives after the user toggles it. This boundary matches the user-facing regression and also makes it possible to keep the native input issue separate. However, it cannot answer the recovery strategy; the control itself is not the source of cross-platform state.

The third was centered on persistence. Here, the first question is how existing Pay Card state is retained, read, and restored, followed by whether the host passes the restored state correctly into the control. This avoids mistaking "the current screen is correct" for "it will still be correct on the next entry," but if adopted alone, the reachability of native input would be reduced to a secondary issue.

The decision after review was not to choose one overall entry point from the three, but to use the boundary between the second and third: ToggleRow Native Input is checked as the interaction object, and Cross-Platform Pay Card Persistence is checked as the state-restoration object; registry remains the lookup entry for types and registrations. This decision limits the judgment path; it does not predetermine which specific file must own which part of the implementation.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Native input
  Native input --> Toggle result
  Toggle result --> State restoration check
  State restoration check --> Host entry point check
  Host entry point check --> [*]
```

The arrows in the diagram indicate the review order, not the runtime call chain. First confirm whether the user completed a toggle, then see how that result appears after recovery, and finally return to the host entry point to determine whether both platforms received the same interpretation of the state. This order comes from splitting the failed merged approach in the initial draft; it does not repackage the three objects into a new module.

## Decisions made

1. **Do not substitute registration types for behavioral judgment.** `devtools/registry/src/types.ts` can be used to find the types, labels, and validation adjacency related to the registration of DevTools, but it must not be used to determine implementation ownership for the native component, persistence, or host wiring.

2. **Validate native input separately.** The issue with ToggleRow first comes down to whether the user can perform a clear toggle. Until this step is confirmed, state differences observed later cannot be directly attributed to persistence.

3. **Validate recovery separately.** Cross-Platform Pay Card Persistence needs to be traced through the actual state-restoration entry point. A successful in-screen toggle cannot serve as substitute evidence that recovery is correct; conversely, a normal display after recovery cannot prove that the native input path has been covered.

4. **Keep host wiring in a separate record.** onboarding Bulk Toggle Semantics and Cross-Platform Host Wiring have their own interface discussion, which should continue in DOC-22. This page only retains the locations to revisit when they intersect with the two boundaries above; it does not re-decide the semantics of batch toggling here.

This decision has a less convenient consequence: regression records must clearly state whether the observation occurred "immediately after toggling" or "after recovery." Previously, writing only "toggle state is inconsistent" was insufficient to distinguish the two types of issue. If native input did not actually trigger a toggle, it is a control-path issue; if the toggle occurred and then changed after recovery, only then should persistence and host wiring be checked.

## Counterexamples retained during review

"Same switch" was once the most misleading description. It compressed the row on the screen, the current in-memory state, and the restored state into one object. For readers, this saved a few lines of explanation; for troubleshooting, however, it produced two bad results.

First, seeing a state change would prompt an immediate investigation along the recovery path. If the native input of ToggleRow did not pass the user's action to the upper layer, the subsequent recovery check would only produce a series of irrelevant observations. Second, seeing a correct recovery result would lead people to treat the input path as covered. Recovery can come from existing state; it cannot show that the user completed a valid toggle on the native end.

Another rejected approach was to put all judgments into the registry's type constraints. zod and the component types do make registry entries easier to read, but they express what shape an entry may have, not the causality between a particular user action and subsequent recovery. Using them as an index is appropriate; using them to finalize behavioral conclusions would make later readers mistakenly believe that the type file already covers the runtime path.

These counterexamples changed how this page is written: instead of using "cross-platform consistency" as a broad conclusion, it records which boundary the current review has reached. That way, even if a new host entry point is found later, there is no need to revisit and invalidate the local judgment about native input.

## Current verification entry points

Start from `devtools/registry/src/types.ts` to trace back the local declaration of the registered object, confirming that the reading target has not been mixed with other DevTools objects. Then route by issue: for issues involving ToggleRow, trace how the user's action becomes a toggle; for cross-platform state, trace the interpretation before and after recovery; for onboarding batch operations or controls provided by the host, move to the interface discussion in DOC-22.

Here, "finding the type" is not treated as "finding the implementation." There may be multiple layers of references between the registry layer and the concrete control and state layers, and the current material does not provide a complete call graph. The review should continue after the actual entry point is found, rather than having this decision record fill in ownership that has not been established.

A quality regression record must retain at least two points in time: the immediate result after the user toggles, and the result after re-entry or after the other platform reads it. If the two are consistent, this only shows that the observation did not expose a difference; if they are inconsistent, first separate them according to the boundaries on this page, then decide whether the issue needs to be brought into the host-wiring discussion.

- We have not confirmed which caller is still using Cross-Platform Pay Card Persistence, or which version and entry point it actually uses.
- We have not confirmed whether a single native toggle of ToggleRow also changes onboarding-related state, or only changes the card configuration.
- If recovery overwrote the toggle that had just been completed, the existing material cannot distinguish whether the overwrite occurred during state reading, recovery merging, or host parameter passing.
- The labels, component types, and validation shapes in registry can help locate the object, but no cross-platform implementation-ownership table has yet been established.

These questions do not change the boundary decisions already made. They show that the next review needs to fill in the specific callers and the actual state path, rather than merging native input and persistence back into one generalized toggle issue.

## Note on the old approach

The initial draft once suggested, "First let all platforms share the same toggle conclusion, then handle recovery." This is no longer applicable. It incorrectly wrote the regression order as the implementation order and also overlooked that host entry points may interpret state independently. This section is retained to prevent someone from later adopting the same merged judgment from the old record.

The only durable conclusion at present is: native input, state recovery, and host wiring can be checked consecutively in the same regression, but they are not the same decision point. For each new symptom, first identify which segment it falls into, then add the corresponding entry.

# Bulk Toggle Wiring Proposal

The first draft made "the host can update all the steps in one go" sound too much like the host needed to understand onboarding's internal state. After review, we narrowed the trial scope: the host only handles the entry point and result display; the onboarding model still owns the step set, order, and completion progress. This lets Web and native screens be wired differently without having each UI interpret the bulk operation independently.

The review still starts at `apps/ledger-live-mobile/src/mvvm/features/DevTools/screens/DevToolsScreen/useDevToolsScreenViewModel.ts`. The `useMemo`, safe area, navigation option types, and theme dependencies visible here show that this entry point itself involves screen-level composition. The trial does not make it the owner of onboarding state; it only needs to receive enough controls to hand off to each platform's screens for binding.

## What the bulk actions mean

This proposal defines only two actions: set all available steps in the current onboarding to complete, or set them all to incomplete. The caller passes an explicit target value; it must not toggle each step based on that step's current value. That approach produces different results on repeated clicks, screen remounts, or opening the two platforms in succession, and a single call cannot tell us what should ultimately be displayed.

Single-step toggling stays on the onboarding side. Bulk and single-step actions share the same step state, and both the completed count and whether all steps are complete are recalculated from that state. The host does not cache the completed count or assemble a result itself from the checked states shown on screen. The stable step order should still be used for display; bulk operations must not change list positions.

If the step set includes temporarily unavailable items, don't have the host guess whether to backfill them or skip them. The trial API should include the "available step set" in the model's response; bulk operations cover only that set. If unavailable steps also need to be written into state later, behavior when they become available again must be defined separately, not quietly folded into this round of bulk toggling.

## Host wiring responsibilities

Both Web and native should read the onboarding snapshot and bulk-action entry point from their respective DevTools control surfaces. The host is responsible for rendering buttons, passing user actions to the model, and refreshing the screen after the model returns a new snapshot. The host is not responsible for wrapping a series of single-step calls into a bulk action or synchronizing a local copy across platforms.

This arrangement has two direct costs. First, the host side needs to wait for the binding layer to provide a complete set of controls; it cannot build the button first with just a boolean. Second, if the native screen still shows an old snapshot on re-entry, the issue should be traced to state restoration or binding refresh, rather than masked by running the bulk action again. Investigations into tour state restoration and package compatibility scope can still refer to the records in DOC-23, but that page's handling procedure is not being incorporated here.

We did not adopt "each host maintains its own select-all state." It would reduce the amount of step data passed, but Web and native would end up with different completion progress for the same bulk operation. We also did not adopt "the host loops through single-step toggle calls": it depends on the number and order of steps, and if a refresh occurs midway, there is no way to tell whether the remaining calls belong to an old request or a new one.

## Trial scope and rollback

The trial is initially limited to the onboarding controls in DevTools; it does not change other entry points for feature tours, balance filtering, or Pay Card. Checks need to cover three things: whether setting to complete twice in a row keeps the steps complete; whether setting to incomplete returns completion progress to the corresponding state; and whether the displayed steps still come from the model snapshot after switching hosts or re-entering the screen.

If a platform can only implement this by toggling steps individually, or cannot restore the same result after re-entering the screen, withdraw the bulk-action entry point on that platform rather than treating a platform-specific patch as shared semantics. Keep the single-step controls, and wait until the host binding shape and restoration boundaries are clear before expanding.

Still undecided are how unavailable steps should be represented in bulk-request responses, and whether the host needs to show the reason for partial completion. Both interface decisions need to wait until we see the data the binding layer actually provides.

# Tour Restoration and Package Boundary Troubleshooting Tree

This page retains an earlier line of investigation. The report placed "the tour reappears" and "the entry-point results do not match" within the same failure boundary, and later reviews still showed these two descriptions intertwined. They may look the same on screen: the feature tour appears again after entering Pay Card; but the former requires tracing how the tour's viewed state is marked and restored, while the latter requires tracing the package entry point used by the caller. Do not merge the two cases into a single state reset just because they ultimately land on the same page.

The initial draft listed `runtime-stubs/feature-tour-state/index.ts` as the restoration entry point. That record has not been deleted, because the issue name and call name at the time did indeed lead the investigation here; it should now be treated as an old navigation point, not a confirmed implementation location. This path can provide local declarations and clues about adjacent code. Finding state with the same name, a forwarding layer, or an old name only means that references need further investigation, not that the tour state can be assumed to be saved or restored here.

The branches below are still suitable for on-call use, but the old habit of "fixing the stub first" no longer applies.

```text
The tour appears again, or the caller's results differ from the example
|
+-- The tour's display changes with the same entry method
|   |
|   +-- The viewed state has not changed as expected
|   |   `-- First check whether the close/complete action reaches the state; do not add restoration logic first.
|   |
|   +-- The state has changed, but the tour still appears on re-entry
|   |   `-- Retain the state after marking and the state read on re-entry.
|   |
|   `-- A reset was performed in this case
|       `-- Do not use this sample to assess restoration; obtain another entry record without a state reset.
|
+-- Direct file access and the caller's entry point produce different results
|   |
|   +-- Only the file path has been checked
|   |   `-- Find the import location actually used in the report before comparing.
|   |
|   +-- The example reference differs from the actual import
|   |   `-- Keep both references side by side to distinguish an entry-point choice difference from an object-shape difference.
|   |
|   `-- The local results could not be used further
|       `-- Do not adjust the compatibility assessment based on those results.
|
`-- The case cannot be reproduced, or the evidence is incomplete
    `-- Record the entry method and current references, and stop expanding the scope of changes.
```

## Preserve the Original State First

Here, "restoration" refers only to whether the previously viewed state is read on re-entry after leaving and affects the tour's display. It is not the same as the user closing the tour, nor is it the same as clearing the state. Before starting, record at least the entry method used in the report, the display before and after entry, and whether any reset occurred in between. If any of these is missing, subsequent comparisons will conflate different states as "restoration failure".

The most common misjudgment in earlier cases was: reset first, then enter, see the tour appear, and attribute the result to the restoration flow. This sequence has been retained as an obsolete practice. Resetting erases the state at the start of the report, making "the action did not mark the state", "the state was not saved", and "the saved state was not read back" all produce the same screen. When a reset needs testing, retain it as a separate sample, not as a replacement for the original sample.

If no change in the viewed state is observed before or after entry, first trace the close or complete action through to the tour's state layer. There is no need to check package exports or balance logic at the same time. Manually writing a seemingly correct state cannot answer whether the original action reached the state layer either; it only hides the point where the flow breaks.

Only if the state has changed but the tour still appears on re-entry should the focus shift to the relationship between the restoration read and the display decision. Preserve two points in time: the state after the marking action, and the state actually read on re-entry. If they differ, continue examining the restoration operations; if they are the same but the display is still abnormal, do not attribute it directly to Redux persistence, and Tour Visibility Model also remains within the scope of investigation.

To navigate to the current tour object, start from the old stub path, then follow the actual references. `features/flow/pay-card-feature-tour/src/state/slice.ts` provides the viewed state and its marking, reset, and restoration operations; `features/flow/pay-card-feature-tour/src/components/FeatureTour/useFeatureTourViewModel.ts` provides visibility, analytics tracking, and close operations. Related names do not mean the two are interchangeable: the former is where state actions land, while the latter handles display and user actions. When both are referenced, record who uses each, rather than treating a single filename as the entire restoration flow.

## The Package Boundary Branch

When the report says "the real entry point and the example produce inconsistent results", do not first make the local screen work by directly referencing internal files. Obtaining an object through direct file access only shows that the file can be opened in the current environment; whether the caller goes through the same entry point and receives the same return shape remains unanswered. Package boundary issues are most easily hidden by direct source access.

First retain two references: the actual import location for the caller used in the report, and the import location used by the example. Until the two are side by side, do not change exports, change state names, or describe the issue as a compatibility regression. If the two are confirmed to come from different entry points, continue distinguishing whether the difference lies in entry-point selection, the returned object, or call timing; without an object comparison, do not guess that it is a version issue.

The old notes contained a shortcut judgment: being able to see the object through the state stub means there is no package boundary issue. That judgment later ceased to apply. A stub is a clue, not the caller's contract. Having the caller bypass the package entry point and directly reference internal files will only keep the example and the real entry point diverging, and cannot establish the compatibility scope of the original report.

The compatibility scope here covers only the tour state and caller entry-point results in this report. Do not use this as a reason to change the feature flag, balance filtering, or other Pay Card features. If the case actually turns into Balance Filter Restoration Boundaries, go to DOC-24; both pages may require retaining the entry method, but they do not share state objects or entry points.

## Traces Left by Follow-up Cards

CARD-213 requires running the source code for "Tour State Restoration Boundary" from the report unchanged on the current version, and circling the specific syntactic units that were changed. This requirement should come after an original sample is available in the state branch: first preserve the actions from the old report, then compare the current references. After the existing implementation was reviewed, the card was later transferred to the current module maintainer, and work began. This indicates that further checking by the module team was needed at the time, not that the cause of the restoration issue had been determined.

CARD-230 corresponds to the other branch: run "Package Boundaries and Compatibility Scope" through the usual entry point, and retain terminal output and workspace side effects separately. The two cannot be collapsed into "ran successfully". Terminal output is information provided at runtime, while workspace side effects are the actual changes left after the run; one being normal does not automatically prove that the other is normal. Work on the card was blocked by the CI queue, and the local results were not used further for subsequent assessments at the time, so this page still treats that check as incomplete evidence.

The two cards share a narrow restriction: without the entry point from the report, do not start fixing anything. CARD-213 requires comparing the old report with the actual references in the current code; CARD-230 requires saving the output and side effects from the usual entry point separately. Neither is permission to "change the state first, then look at the screen".

## What to Record Under Each Branch

The state branch only needs the following facts, not a full incident table:

- The entry method used in the report, and whether re-entry used the same entry point;
- The viewed state before marking, after marking, and on re-entry;
- Whether a reset was performed, and whether the original sample is still available;
- Whether the close or complete action has reached the state layer.

For the entry-point branch, retain the actual import location, the example's reference location, terminal output, and workspace side effects. Do not fill in state names, import results, or persistence locations that have not been observed. For tour restoration, the most valuable evidence is where the state changes; for package boundaries, it is the side-by-side references to the two entry points. Mixing them into one record makes it easy for the next person taking over to mistake a single display change for proof of compatibility.

The current round can stop in the following cases: the report only says the tour reappeared but provides no entry method; only a state change is available, without the read result on re-entry; only the stub has been opened, without finding the caller's import; the example and caller entry points have not been placed side by side; or the local check was interrupted and there is no new complete result. Stopping does not mean the anomaly has disappeared, only that the available evidence is insufficient to determine the restoration boundary or package boundary.

The old path from the initial draft retained above is still worth opening, but its only role is to bring people close to the current references. Exactly where the viewed state is saved, and why the example entry point differs from the real entry point, remain two unresolved questions on this page. One adjacent question has not yet been split out: when both entry points can display the tour, will their differences also affect the state update after closing; there is currently not enough evidence to answer.

This page was originally written around "which person to find first after the directory gets stuck," but later people kept putting different situations into the same path. The current entry may expose only a directory card, or the stuck point may appear only after entering `web/native entrypoint`. Do not merge the two cases: for the former, confirm the entry first; for the latter, first preserve the first anomalous location within the entry.

At the start, leave four things behind: the text that actually appeared on the page, whether the entry is web or native, the first visible result, and the environment differences before and after rerunning. If any item is missing, you can only add a record; you cannot treat the directory title or a single green rerun as an explanation.

```text
Stuck point seen from Current entry
├─ No original record
│  ├─ Only a directory name, screenshot, or handoff request
│  │  └─ Add the first visible result; stop
│  └─ Cannot even confirm the entry form
│     └─ Find web/native entrypoint; stop
└─ Has an original record
   ├─ Can find the most recent normal Pay Card sample
   │  ├─ Sample entry differs: verify the entry first
   │  ├─ Sample environment differs: verify the environment first
   │  ├─ The first difference is still in DevTools: stay in the project
   │  └─ The first difference crosses a clearly defined interface: hand off to the shared owner
   └─ Cannot find a sample under the same conditions
      └─ Keep both inputs; do not close out based on the rerun result
```

The tree's purpose is to stop at places where there is no evidence. It is not meant to have the person taking over guess from "stuck" all the way to the ultimate cause. When there is no original record, the troubleshooting action is to add the original record; when there is no normal sample under the same conditions, "cannot compare" is itself the result left by this investigation. Do not fill the blanks with adjacent cards, similar directory names, or business terms that appeared later just to complete the branch.

## The old nodes are still here

The first version had a very short path: first look for `web/native entrypoint` in `docs/adj-devtools/runbooks/devtools-compatibility-catalog-who-to-escalate-to-when-blocked.md`, then, after seeing `DevTools`, continue looking for `Redux persistence`. If persistence does not appear, stop.

This old wording was not removed. It explains why someone stopped at `DevTools` at the time, and why later records treated persistence as a prominent checkpoint. It does not prove that a stuck directory is necessarily caused by persistence, much less that web and native fail at the same location. When following the old path yields "did not see `Redux persistence`," retain that fact only; do not rewrite it as a recovery conclusion.

Early records also tended to retry first. Later, it became clear that a green result after a retry only shows that that rerun produced a result; the original entry, the original first failure location, and the original environment differences may still have been lost. Therefore, this page later required preserving the initial failure sample first. This addendum does not say that retrying is useless; it only cannot replace the original incident context.

Another old judgment was, "If it matches the normal Pay Card sample, check the environment or entry; if it does not match, stop at DevTools." This wording remains, but at the time it did not make clear whether the two samples came from the same entry. If one came from a directory card and the other had already entered `web/native entrypoint`, they cannot be routed directly based on whether they match. The comparison must start from the first difference, not from the final page or the directory display.

## Current recording order

First open `docs/adj-devtools/runbooks/devtools-compatibility-catalog-who-to-escalate-to-when-blocked.md`. Do not search only for the directory title; locate `web/native entrypoint` in the file, then record which side was actually hit this time. If the entry is not matched, stop at the entry record and do not look for downstream terms.

Once the entry is confirmed, save the first visible result. This may be an anomaly on the directory card, or a stuck point that appears only after entering the entry; record the two separately. Do not organize the screenshots first, and do not run a second time first and then fill in the text for the first run. Record environment differences only when an on-site comparison already exists; do not guess any environment state.

Next, find the most recent normal Pay Card sample. When comparing, change only one condition: if comparing the entry, do not change the environment at the same time; if comparing the environment, do not change the input at the same time. If this comparison cannot be made, leave the two inputs side by side. Average results, directory names, and the final display can all be clues, but they are not used to determine what happened at an intermediate node.

If the first difference is at the entry, continue checking the entry; if the first difference is in the environment, continue checking the environment. If the difference is still within the records, permissions, or index scope of `DevTools`, continue having devtools · Compatibility Catalog handle it. Only when the difference crosses a project interface that has already been clearly recorded should it be handed off to the shared owner. When the interface location has not been recorded, do not replace the record with "it looks like an external issue."

## Words easily mistaken for causes

Later addenda once placed `Card API extra`, `stablecoin balance`, `feature flag override`, `action tile`, `mobile store`, and `analytics event` near the same tree. They came from different investigation passes and are not an interchangeable set of diagnostic results.

When you see `Card API extra`, first check whether the original record really stopped at that node; without a direct excerpt, you can only record that the term appeared. `stablecoin balance` also cannot automatically show that the issue has left the directory. `feature flag override` only indicates that someone once investigated along the switch direction; it does not replace an entry or environment comparison.

The same handling applies to `action tile`, `mobile store`, and `analytics event`: they may be terms that appeared in the incident, or they may simply be indexes added later at the margin. Without a call excerpt and the first difference, do not hand off based on them. `balance filter` was once written as the endpoint of part of an investigation, and a later record wrote `Card API extra` as the endpoint; neither endpoint proves the other, and neither alone can determine who takes over.

## Notes beside the card

CARDA-003 is used to look back at the objective of Current entry and the last confirmation. The handoff was confirmed, and later the action assignee changed because the testing phase needed someone who could modify fixtures. This change only explains why the person was changed at that time; do not write that person as the directory's long-term owner.

CARDA-008 is used to return from a directory or report to the original record for the current revision. The baseline had already been recorded, and the card had also entered processing; but one public note pointed out that the person on duty had replied to the previous item, not to this card. When encountering adjacent records, first confirm the card number and failure location, then decide whether to include it in the current incident. Do not merge two records merely because they are adjacent.

CARDA-013 is suitable only for recording a temporary takeover action. It only began being handled after a documentation check, and still cannot be used to infer that the maintenance entry has a stable owner. When someone needs to take over, hand over the current branch: for example, add the entry record, add a comparison sample, or confirm the permission scope; do not hand over the entire tree together with the root cause.

## Stop points

When the resources, permissions, or indexes still belong to devtools · Compatibility Catalog, continue within the project. If a subsequent action requires changing the user-visible contract of Pay Card, stop this page and move to formal review. This stop point is more important than "find someone to continue investigating first," because the latter can easily bring a guess with no interface record outside the project.

If the entry cannot be confirmed, stop at the entry; if the first result cannot be confirmed, stop at the first result; if the normal sample cannot be confirmed, stop at the sample comparison; if the interface location cannot be confirmed, stop at the interface location. The old path may still lead someone to `Redux persistence`, and may still cause someone to retry first. These are historical judgments left by this record, not verified recovery actions.

Finally, retain the original input, the first visible result, the entry type, and the first difference. If any one of them is missing, do not fill in a seemingly reasonable root cause, and do not write the temporary assignee as the long-term owner.

Recovery of the user path could only narrow the impact of the first observation, not answer the other two questions as well.

Pay Card was still working normally during the checks, which was the basis for narrowing the scope at the time. The stablecoin balance subsequently recovered, showing that the balance state could not be used as evidence of a prolonged split in the catalog state. Both observations affected only the assessment of "which paths did not reproduce the initial discrepancy"; they did not show that the schema generation mechanism was now correct, nor that all callers had adopted the migration records again.

## Wrong Directions Taken Along the Way

At one point, the issue was thought to involve the reversed order of the indexing time and `devtools-compatibility-catalog`. This line of investigation came from the records for CARDA-010. The card later confirmed the maintainer, but the retained description still said that the "due action" referred to yesterday's object. That sentence looked more like a mismatch in the object the record referred to: it suggested checking the order of indexing and catalog references, but could not by itself prove that catalog generation or the migration process had gone wrong.

Another earlier assessment attributed the discrepancy to an adjacent path. There was not enough evidence for this either. The Pay Card path was still working normally during the same checks, and the stablecoin balance subsequently recovered; therefore, the claim that "adjacent projects caused all the anomalies" was retained as speculation from that time, rather than a postmortem conclusion. The earlier assessment was not deleted because it explained why the initial comparison scope had been drawn too broadly.

Some also interpreted the entry point becoming available again as meaning that the two states had merged. Later caller-side observations partially contradicted this interpretation: the entry point could recover so that it no longer showed the initial discrepancy, while the caller could still be stuck waiting for a result. The two observations concerned different stages, so a green result on one side could not be used to draw a conclusion about the other.

## Review Methods That Failed

Previously, only a screenshot had been forwarded. The screenshot showed two states, but had no account, version, or run id, so the states could not be correlated with the time at which the entry point was observed; it also did not explain why the other path was working normally. Whoever took over could only guess at the impact scope again, without being able to determine whether they were seeing an old index, an old record, or a caller result that was still pending.

A caller-side follow-up check was later performed through the original entry point. The observation recorded for CARDA-015 was: the exit entry point opens, but once at the current result, it keeps showing a spinner. This result did not contradict the record that "the user path has recovered", because the two statements referred to different stages: the entry point no longer showing the initial discrepancy did not mean that the waiting caller had received a result. The materials contained no usable combination of versions to establish the correspondence, so the waiting was not attributed to any particular package or migration.

The follow-up check for CARDA-015 originally called only for selecting one adjacent current revision with a working path and comparing the first path difference. It did not call for establishing the full caller chain, nor did it provide a second equivalent path on which to base a conclusion. Treating this follow-up check as confirmation of the cause would go beyond the evidence preserved at the time.

Two types of comparison were retained after recovery: whether the catalog entry point and the old record still showed different current revision values; and whether the caller was still stuck at the same result stage. What could be confirmed was that the original evidence, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause should be preserved separately. What could not be confirmed was the layer at which the analytics event changed, and a single recovery of the stablecoin balance could not establish that compatibility had been fully restored after migration.

## Maintenance Records Added Later

For CARDA-005, a document check appeared first, followed by scope confirmation. The card's statement that "the temporary assignee handles only due actions and does not define the long-term meaning of the maintenance entry point" preserved the responsibility boundary at the time: taking over did not change who maintained the catalog in the long term, nor could the temporary handling be interpreted as a redefinition of the state contract.

CARDA-010 kept the indexing-time issue separate and confirmed the maintainer. The value of this card was not in providing a root cause, but in preventing the object referenced yesterday and the current catalog from being mixed into the same handling record. The gap in entry-point ownership in CARDA-005, the timing mismatch in CARDA-010, and the caller waiting in CARDA-015 are three distinct outstanding items, and cannot be pieced together into a complete causal chain.

The earlier evidence for the compatibility catalog can be reviewed using the following relationships:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Diverged: Entry point differs from old record
    Diverged --> Compared: Compare Pay Card and DevTools
    Compared --> Restored: User path recovers
    Compared --> Pending: Current result still pending
    Restored --> Pending: Caller continues follow-up checks
    Pending --> Compared: New entry point or record arrives
```

In the diagram, `Pending` is only a place to record the observation that "the current result keeps showing a spinner", not a new state definition for the catalog, nor an indication that the root cause has been found. Likewise, `Restored` records only the recovery of the user path. The two nodes can exist in sequence precisely because the entry-point review and the caller waiting have not been shown to be the same issue in these materials.

## Scope Retained to Date

This postmortem can describe a split in the state of a compatibility catalog entry point, how the impact was narrowed, when the user path recovered, and which assessments later lacked supporting evidence. It cannot explain the full schema generation mechanism or migration batches, or confirm that a specific fix for any caller has been completed. The full production-side combination of versions was not preserved in this incident evidence either.

The original file remains the starting point for review: `docs/adj-devtools/incidents/devtools-compatibility-catalog-two-states-for-one-object.md`. This entry point preserves the anomaly materials from that time, rather than recertifying the current catalog state. Changes unrelated to the compatibility catalog were not included; observations from adjacent projects were not added as part of this incident either.

The correspondence among the indexing time, the analytics event, caller waiting, and the two current revision values remains unconfirmed. In particular, "the exit entry point opens" and "the current result keeps showing a spinner" cannot be reduced to a simple available or unavailable status: the former is the entry point reached during the follow-up check, and the latter is the waiting observed afterward. If two states appear again, at least the entry-point time, the old record, and the caller result should be preserved side by side; preserving only the final recovery screen would recreate the initial gap.

This page still retains earlier claims such as reversed indexing order and attribution to adjacent paths because they document the misinterpretations at the time, not because those claims have been proven again.

Use this checklist when preparing to exit the ledger-live-desktop-release-automation window and the person on duty only needs to verify the exit actions, the last visible result, and the actions left on the desktop side. "Exit" here follows the old window's criteria: first confirm that routing no longer takes people back to the old action, then check the last renderer record. Release success is not determined here; the relevant owner still signs off on that separately.

## Checks Within the Window

1. Open `docs/adj-ledger-live-desktop/release/ledger-live-desktop-release-automation-exit-window-checklist.md` and look for this exit action, starting from `analytics event`. If that record is missing, do not substitute an entry point with a similar name; leave the window blank and stop at this step.

4. Check `cross-package export`. If this item has not appeared, stop further cleanup and do not mark the renderer result as complete. The old window allows only a "waiting for export" status; a missing record does not mean export has already gone through.

- The last visible result cannot be matched to the current route;
- `desktop renderer` still shows the old action, but the routing snapshot has been deleted;
- `cross-package export` is missing, or its name can only be matched by guessing.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Caller Integration Blockers

This page starts at the current entry point. First obtain the last verifiable state before the failure, then decide whether to continue investigating domain-client-integration or hand the incident evidence over beyond the permissions boundary. Here, "handoff" does not mean passing along a vaguely defined failure; it must include at least the original input, current revision, first visible result, and first confirmed difference.

## Preserve the Incident State First

The previous version only said, "Continue once there is a record." That sentence is not enough when actually taking over. Missing records usually fall into two cases: nothing was collected at the time, or only a clean rerun result was retained afterward. Neither case allows you to move straight to discussing the root cause.

```text
Does the current entry point have an original record?
├─ No
│  ├─ The state one step before the failure can be recovered
│  │  └─ Recover it, then start from the first difference
│  └─ It cannot be recovered
│     └─ Mark as unknown and stop; do not replace the original incident state with a new green result
└─ Yes
   ├─ The original input, current revision, and first visible result are all present
   │  └─ Compare adjacent samples
   └─ Any one of these is missing
      └─ Fill in the missing item first, without attributing a cause
```

The work item in CARDD-002 is to recover the state at the current entry point before the failure. What must be recovered is the last verifiable state, not a normal-looking fragment selected after the fact. CARDD-004 require attaching the domain-client-integration from that time, the current entry point, and the first visible current revision back to this page; this is also the minimum starting point for this tree. If these materials cannot all be provided together, the person taking over can only know that "it worked normally at some later point," not where it was originally blocked.

When preserving the incident state, do not splice two execution records into one. Each record must retain its own input and visible result. Later green results can be appended to show what happened afterward, but cannot overwrite the first result. This is also why CARDD-013 refer to the first recorded current revision after the change: find it first, then discuss whether subsequent behavior is stable.

## Compare Only as Far as the First Difference

Once the incident state has been preserved, take one sample from an adjacent domain-client-integration for comparison. CARDD-008 require changing only this one adjacent input, leaving the current entry point and entry point otherwise unchanged. This does not provide a complete explanation, only a point from which to investigate further.

```text
Did the comparison with the adjacent input change only one item?
├─ Yes
│  ├─ The first difference is still in the integration-testing input or project-internal state
│  │  └─ Stay in domain-client-integration, and continue checking that item
│  └─ The first difference crosses a clearly defined interface
│     └─ Record the interface and sample, and hand off to the permissions owner on the other side of the interface
└─ No
   ├─ The difference comes from the environment
   │  └─ Retain the environmental difference together with the sample, and exit this comparison
   └─ The source of the difference is unknown
      └─ Stop, and do not treat the average case as a conclusion
```

"Adjacent" only means that this input is sufficient for a local comparison, not that it is a substitute for the same incident state. If the comparison requires changing the entry point, input, and environment together, there is no single difference to use for routing; in that case, do not classify it as a caller issue just because a rerun succeeded, and do not hand it to an external maintainer just because the directory contains a similar name.

The verification method in CARDD-006 is to have an actual consumer read through to the current revision via the original entry point, stopping at the first difference. The output of this action should be a specific stopping point, not a blanket statement that "the consumer has verified it." If the stopping point is still within this project, the integration maintainers continue handling it; if it crosses a clearly defined interface, hand it off together with the sample. If the consumer can only read a later state, still treat this as a missing-record case.

## Three Exit Routes Before Handoff

The first exit route is to stay in domain-client-integration. This applies when the first difference is still an input, resource, or permissions state that this project can confirm. Record the current node and continue filling in the facts for that node; do not follow speculation into an external implementation.

The second exit route is the permissions owner. This applies when the first difference has already crossed a clearly defined interface, and further assessment requires permissions or materials from the other side of the interface. The handoff must include only the current entry point, original input, current revision, first visible result, adjacent sample, and interface name. Do not use this exit route without an interface name.

The third exit route is to exit. This applies when there is no original record, the comparison changed more than one condition, environmental differences cannot be narrowed down, or whether collection and execution have even occurred is still unconfirmed. Exiting does not mean closing the issue; it means the tree on this page cannot proceed any further using the available materials. CARDD-015 require the current revision to remain unknown until collection or execution has actually occurred.

```text
Where is the first difference?
├─ Within integration testing
│  └─ Stay within the project, and fill in the materials for that node
├─ Beyond a clearly defined interface
│  └─ Hand off to the permissions owner, with the interface and sample attached
└─ The location cannot be confirmed
   └─ Exit; retain the unknown status and the gaps in the incident evidence
```

## Two Paths That Are Easy to Take by Mistake

The old records contain one premature retry. The result after the retry looked more complete, but the first failing input was not retained, so the comparison target changed from the original incident state to a different execution. This path is now retained here: reruns can help generate new samples, but cannot fill in the intermediate steps of an old sample after the fact.

The other path is to infer intermediate states backward from the final display, directory names, or average results. This information can suggest where to look next, but cannot explain why the first visible result appeared. In particular, when the same execution record gives two values, first retain both values and the locations where they appear. CARDD-008 previously added a note that the same execution record gave two values at 14:32 and 14:47; until the difference has been narrowed down, do not choose one of them as the sole input.

## What to Write When Taking Over

The handoff entry can be short, but it must let the next person reach the same stopping point:

- The symptoms visible at the current entry point at the time;
- Whether both the original input and current revision are present;
- The first visible result, not a later green rerun result;
- Whether only one item was changed in the adjacent sample;
- The first difference, or an explicit statement that it is unconfirmed;
- The reason for staying within the project, handing off to the permissions owner, or exiting.

There is no need to merge every adjacent issue into this page. CARDD-004, CARDD-006, CARDD-008, and CARDD-015 retain the entry points for supplementing incident records, verification by an actual consumer, single-variable replay, and unknown states, respectively; this page only organizes them into a handoff tree. DOC-42 retain incident notes for unresolved cases, and you can refer back to that page at a node with no new evidence, but do not use it to fabricate samples that this page does not have.

The maintenance entry point is still `docs/adj-domain/runbooks/domain-client-integration-who-to-escalate-to-when-blocked.md`. Starting here, the tree stops at the first point where new evidence is needed.

# Caller Integration Blocker Troubleshooting Tree

When the current entry point stalls, first treat it as an integration-testing incident whose cause has not yet been pinpointed, rather than a name awaiting assignment. The person taking over starts from the last confirmable state before the failure; if they can confirm the first difference, they continue from that point; if they cannot, they leave the unknown where it is. This sequence may seem slow, but it actually prevents a later rerun, a similar directory, or a final display from being mistaken for the original incident.

The entry file is `docs/adj-domain/runbooks/domain-client-integration-who-to-escalate-to-when-blocked.md`. The person taking over is not expected to identify every cause at once, only to be able to answer each time: what records are currently in hand, what the comparison changed, and why the next step still belongs to this project, why a permissions owner is needed, or why they should exit.

## Collect Only Four Things Before Starting

Do not start by asking "Whose problem is this". First confirm whether you have these four things: the original input, the current revision, the first visible result, and the last confirmable state before the failure. They are not a set of attachments that must all be present before you can start writing; a missing item is itself a branch in the tree. The point is that when an item is missing, you must not fill the gap with after-the-fact impressions.

The original input is the input sent into domain-client-integration at the time. The current revision identifies the version in use at the time. The first visible result means the earliest result left on record, however inconvenient later reruns, revisions, or overwrites may have made it. The last confirmable state before the failure defines exactly what could still be confirmed before things "stalled". If any of the four items is missing, explicitly state which one is missing rather than vaguely saying "the incident context is incomplete".

```text
Start from the current entry point
│
├─ Have the original input, current revision, first recorded result, and pre-failure state
│  └─ Proceed to adjacent-sample comparison
│
├─ One item is missing, but it can be recovered from the same incident
│  └─ Recover it first; after recovery, still compare using the first recorded result
│
└─ One item is missing, and it cannot be proven to come from the same incident
   └─ Stop at the unknown; do not substitute a later execution
```

CARDD-002 describe the first kind of backfill: backfill one step before the current entry point, recording the last confirmable state before the failure. This does not require reorganizing the entire history into a clean sample. CARDD-004 further require linking the domain-client-integration from that time, the current entry point, and the current revision as first seen back to this record. Only with both items linked together can someone taking over later know where things originally started, rather than merely knowing that someone looked here afterward.

If all that remains at the current entry point is a single successful rerun, first label it separately as a follow-up sample. It can show that an execution took place later, but must not be written back as "the original issue was reproduced and then resolved". If only the final display remains at the current entry point, first record the source of that final display and the gaps as well; do not work backward from the displayed result to write the intermediate inputs. The same applies if only a directory or name remains: a name can help with lookup, but it is not evidence of an invocation.

## The Starting Point from the Old Version Is Still Retained

The first version left a short rule: continue when there is a record; if there is no record, collect more; only after seeing an adjacent difference decide whether to stay within integration debugging or cross the interface. It did not break "records" down at the time, nor did it explain how a rerun would change the state. This version keeps that concise judgment because many temporary handoffs really do start here; however, later practice showed that saying only "collect more" makes it easy to mistake newly collected information for the old state.

The old wording "continue along one branch first" remains valid. Its meaning is: when the preceding item has no evidence, do not jump to the final cause. The addition now is that the preceding item is not merely an abstract condition but should be tied to one of the original input, the current revision, the first result, or the pre-failure state. Whichever item is missing, stop the branch at that item.

The old version also wrote "if DevTools does not appear, stop here" as an early hint. This hint can no longer serve on its own as a handoff conclusion. Whether a particular adjacent object appears is insufficient to show that the interface has been crossed, nor to establish who the permission belongs to. The current tree hands off only on the basis of a confirmed interface boundary; object names can serve only as clues for finding the relevant materials. This old hint is retained as a historical reminder, to avoid again using visible names in place of call relationships.

## Check the records first; do not run it first

When a state already exists, the most common temptation is to rerun immediately. A rerun is useful, but it produces a second state. Write down the four items from the first state before deciding whether it is worth running a second time. That way, even if the new result is green, it will not mask the node that was originally stuck.

```text
After obtaining a new execution
├─ All four items of the original state are complete
│  ├─ The new execution changes only one condition
│  │  └─ It can serve as an adjacent sample for comparison
│  └─ The new execution changes multiple conditions
│     └─ Save it separately; do not use it to locate the first difference
└─ The four items of the original state are incomplete
   └─ Do not use the new execution to fill in the old state; return to the missing-item branch
```

There was once an overly early retry. What remained afterward was a result that was easier to read, while the original input and intermediate state could no longer be reconstructed. After that experience, the rule changed to prioritize preserving the first failed sample and environmental differences. Here, environmental differences are used only to explain why the two samples cannot be compared directly; they do not automatically point to an external object or constitute a reason for handoff.

When a new sample appears to have "recovered," the record should distinguish at least three things: whether it still uses the original input; whether it is still on the current revision; whether it retains the same current entry point. If any one of the three differs, the new sample is merely a later execution. It can be attached after the original record, but do not change the original result to green or use it to close the original branch.

CARDD-013 focuses on the first current-entry result after a change, precisely to prevent a later green result from overwriting the earliest one. When the person taking over reviews it, first confirm that this result belongs to the current revision after the change; then confirm that it has not been mixed in with subsequent executions. If that cannot be done, continue to leave the version position as unknown.

## The boundary of adjacent samples

Before entering the comparison, first select an adjacent domain-client-integration. Adjacent does not mean identical, nor does it mean "looks the most normal". It only means that the sample is sufficient for someone to start from the current entry point and see the first difference step by step.

CARDD-008 requires changing only one adjacent domain-client-integration, leaving the remaining current entry point and entry unchanged. During execution, write the comparison record within this constraint: first record what remains unchanged, then the only input that was changed, and finally the earliest difference to appear. Do not write a speculative cause first. If the record cannot specify which parts remain unchanged, it cannot confirm that this is a single-variable comparison.

```text
Adjacent sample comparison
│
├─ Only one adjacent input changes
│  ├─ The first difference has appeared
│  │  └─ Record that point and determine whether it is still within the integration-debugging boundary
│  └─ There is no first difference
│     └─ Do not write "no difference observed" as "no problem"
│
├─ The current entry point or environment also changes outside the input
│  └─ Record the environment difference and exit the comparison branch
│
└─ It is impossible to say exactly what changed
   └─ Return to the run and complete the record; do not choose a guess as the difference
```

"Changing only one condition" is not for producing a polished experiment record, but to let the next person recheck the first difference. If the current entry point and adjacent input are changed at the same time, even if the result is obvious, it can only show that the two executions differ; it cannot show which side the difference belongs to. If the environment also changes, write down the environment difference first; if it cannot be narrowed down, exit here.

The approach of CARDD-006 is to have a real user follow the original entry point to read the current revision and stop at the first difference. The stopping location for this action is important: it does not require the user to determine the root cause, does not require the user to vouch for the entire system, and does not require later results to be turned into the original record. The result should be an identifiable stopping point. If the stopping point is still within this project, continue on this page; only when the stopping point has crossed an explicit interface should you prepare a handoff.

If the real user can only see the later state, the original sample cannot be reconstructed retroactively. At this point, you may record "original entry point not restored", but do not call the later state confirmation of the same input. The purpose of adjacent samples is to narrow uncertainty, not eliminate it.

## The first difference determines where to go

After the comparison yields the first difference, do not immediately assign a technical attribution. First look at the boundary where that point lies. The current tree has only three exits, and each exit has a clear stopping point.

```text
Has the first difference been confirmed?
├─ Not yet confirmed
│  └─ Exit: retain the samples, missing items, and environment differences
├─ Within domain-client-integration
│  └─ Stay within the project: continue completing this node's input or state
└─ Crosses an explicit interface
   └─ Hand off to the permission owner: include the interface name and comparison context
```

Staying within the project applies when the first difference is still an input, an in-project resource, or a project-internal permission state that domain-client-integration can confirm. The action here is not to immediately expand the troubleshooting scope, but to complete the materials for that node: what the current entry point is, what the original input is, whether the current revision can be confirmed, and what the initial result is. If the first difference changes location after the materials are completed, reassess it according to the new location.

A handoff to the permissions owner is valid, but only when the comparison has already crossed a clearly identified interface. The handoff should be brief but reviewable: the current entry point, original input, current revision, first visible result, adjacent samples, first difference and interface name. If the interface name is missing, do not replace it with "the other side should handle this". At this point, return to the unknown exit, or continue gathering enough material to confirm the interface.

For the exit action, the applicable cases are when the original records cannot be recovered, the comparison actually changed multiple conditions, environmental differences cannot be narrowed down, or it has not even been confirmed whether collection and execution occurred. Exiting does not mean the issue is resolved, nor does it mean no one needs to keep following up; it means this tree cannot safely determine the next step beyond this point. CARDD-015 require that until collection or execution is confirmed to have actually occurred, the current revision remain unknown. This unknown status should be recorded, rather than filled in with a default version.

## Handling "permissions"

The permissions owner on this page is the person who can address the permissions boundary on the side confirmed to be beyond the interface, not the person who receives the most messages, nor the person whose name is most similar to the object's name. Identify the interface that was crossed before handing off; after handoff the other party decides whether there is enough material on the other side of the interface to proceed. If they need to return to the original input or the first result, the records on this page are still their starting point.

Do not prematurely send project-internal resource or permissions issues outside the project. As long as the first difference is still within a state that domain-client-integration itself can confirm, keep the issue within the project for now and gather more material. Conversely, do not insist on keeping a cross-interface issue here just because this page is for integration debugging; once evidence from beyond a clearly identified interface has appeared, continuing to speculate on this page will only distort the state under investigation.

You can use the following brief handoff entry, without writing a separate lengthy explanation for every handoff:

```text
Current entry point: ……
Original input: Retained / Missing
Current revision: …… / Unconfirmed
First visible result: ……
Adjacent samples: Change only…… / Not a single-variable comparison
First difference: …… / Unconfirmed
Interface: ……
Destination: Continue within the project / Permissions owner / Exit
```

The ellipses are not an invitation to fabricate content. Simply write "Missing" or "Unconfirmed" when no material is available. In particular do not enter a later green result as the first visible result, and do not record a guessed interface name as confirmed.

## Two phenomena that have led to mistaken judgments

The first is "green after a rerun". It can make people feel that the original state no longer matters. In fact, green only proves that the later execution produced a result; if the input, current revision, current entry point or environment has changed, it cannot prove that the original state was restored. The premature retries in the old records are therefore retained on this page, not as recommended actions, but as a reminder that old and new samples must be distinguished when taking over.

The second type is "two values for the same execution record". The addendum to CARDD-008 notes that the same execution record gives two values at 14:32 and 14:47. Both values should be retained until there is enough material to explain why they differ. Do not choose the value that better matches expectations to move the handoff forward, and do not discard the other as noise. At this point, you can continue checking the current entry point and input corresponding to each value; if that cannot be done, the first point of divergence remains unconfirmed.

What these two situations have in common is not a specific implementation, but that both can make the incident context seem more complete than it actually is. The approach is also the same: keep the original records separate from later results, identify the gaps, and stop where new material is needed.

## Revised sequence for taking over

The second version used "Do we have the original records" as the starting point. That starting point is retained, but the sequence is now more narrowly defined to prevent anyone taking over from jumping straight to assigning responsibility:

1. Find the last confirmable state before the failure.
2. Confirm whether the original input, current revision, and first visible result come from the same incident context.
3. If a missing item can be recovered, recover only that item; if it cannot, leave it unknown.
4. Select one adjacent domain-client-integration, and confirm that all other current entry points remain unchanged.
5. Write down the first point of divergence, without assigning a cause first.
6. Continue if the first point of divergence is within the project; hand off to the permissions owner only if it crosses a clearly defined interface; exit if its location is unclear.

This sequence does not require reaching the sixth step every time. Most blocked cases will stop at the first missing item or when a comparison does not hold, which is exactly the boundary this page is intended to preserve. Skipping a stopping point just to move forward usually yields only a conclusion reached faster, but one that cannot be verified later.

## How the card entry point relates to this page

CARDD-002 is the entry point for supplementing the record of the pre-failure state. CARDD-004 is the entry point for linking the three items back to the original case. CARDD-006 is the entry point for verifying the actual consumer's stopping point through the original entry point. CARDD-008 is the entry point for single-variable replays with adjacent inputs and recording both values. CARDD-013 points to the first result after the change. CARDD-015 preserves the current revision state before collection or execution is confirmed.

These cards each retain only local actions. This page does not combine them into a single event, nor does it infer any call details that were not recorded. To view case notes that have not yet been closed out, refer to DOC-42; it provides an entry point to records from adjacent cases and does not replace the handoff decision here.

## Stop conditions after handoff

After handing off to the permissions owner, the work on this page does not become "waiting for results". The record should stop at the confirmed interface boundary. If the other party returns a new sample, first attach it back to the current entry point as new material, then go through the tree again starting with the four checks. Do not interpret new material directly as the answer for the original branch just because the issue has already been handed off.

When the issue stays within the project, continue adding information at that node only if the new material still points to the same first difference. If the new material changes the location of the earliest difference, retain the old assessment as the assessment at the time, and note afterward that it has been superseded by the new material. This makes it clear why a handoff was not pursued at the time and prevents later readers from mistaking the old stopping point for the current interface boundary.

After exiting, the conditions for re-entering this tree are also simple: restore the missing original records, obtain an adjacent sample with only one item changed, or confirm a previously unclear interface. Any other follow-up discussion, similar names, repeated execution, or average results are insufficient to replace the entry conditions.

Finally, review the current entry point: if the record does not allow another maintainer to clearly state "where I stopped, and why I stopped", then the minimum record required by this page is not yet complete. What needs to be added is the stopping point and the gaps, not a guessed conclusion.

# Pay Card Freeze Window Decision Record

This round of freeze discussions did not treat Pay Card as a single desktop entry point. The desktop-side host-bindings entry can remain, but it cannot replace cross-platform comparison; we need to trace the behavior through the actual package export, host calls, and Redux restoration chain before discussing whether the window should be changed.

There were two approaches on the table at the time: retain the existing entry point and freeze the areas already covered, or use the window to adjust the entry point and cross-platform setup. We chose the former. The reason is not that the latter is necessarily wrong, but that the Desktop/Mobile comparison was still only a requirement, and was not enough to support expanding the window into an entry-point change.

Accordingly, this round approves only the scope covered by existing evidence. The comparison results need to be broken down into small conclusions: which package export the host uses, whether the restoration chain passes through the same state, and whether the difference really lies in cross-platform behavior. Any part for which these follow-up checks are incomplete will not be decided as part of the freeze.

"Adjust the window" remains in the record but was not taken as an action in this round. The cost would be mixing the host-call and restoration issues that should have been confirmed first into the release cadence; even if a difference appeared afterward, it would be difficult to tell whether it was an existing difference or one caused by adjusting the window.
