versions.body:
# Pay Card Freeze Window Decision Record

Initially calling this a "freeze window" could make people think this was only about deciding when to stop making changes. The actual debate centered on the entry point: the desktop host already had a usable host-bindings path, so should it be changed within the same window to a new cross-platform arrangement? At the time, the call names around the desktop were repeatedly brought up for a simple reason: people first saw the existing host-side entry point, not the package export, restored state, and corresponding relationship on the other side.

This record preserves the tradeoffs made at the time, not an overview of later entry points. People may still look here later for the statement "retain the current entry point"; it refers only to the scope covered by this freeze. Do not read it as a long-term judgment about all host wiring.

## The Two Paths on the Review Table

**Retain the current host-bindings entry point.**

This did not declare that the entry point had no problems; it treated it as the starting point that could be frozen this round. Existing desktop-side wiring would not be rearranged during the window; the real package export, host calls, and Redux restoration chain would first be aligned segment by segment. If Desktop and Mobile produced different results, the differences would first be written as small conclusions that could be checked separately, rather than immediately attributing the differences to the entry-point design.

**Adjust the window and change the cross-platform arrangement along with it.**

Someone argued for this proposal very directly at the time: since we had to do the Desktop/Mobile comparison, we might as well tidy up the entry point in the same round, so we would not have to come back to it after the freeze. It was not approved. The objection was not a preference for the old interface; it was that the comparison itself had not been completed enough to support this kind of change. Without tracing the real export and host call end to end, the supposed "cross-platform difference" might merely be a comparison of two objects that were not at the same layer; adjusting the window as well would only make the judgment harder to disentangle.

The compromise proposed at the time—"change part of it first, then look at the comparison"—was also not accepted. Partial changes would mix the desktop-side behavior with the state after the change, making it impossible later to say whether the observed restoration difference had already existed. A freeze window is not a suitable place for exploratory refactoring.

## Decision for This Round

The decision was to retain the current host-bindings entry point and freeze only where existing evidence provides coverage. The window would not combine entry-point adjustment and cross-platform comparison into one action.

This sentence has two limitations that were not clear enough in the initial draft and were added here later:

- "Retain" only means that this round will not use entry-point adjustment as an approval condition; it does not mean that the entry point has already been determined to be the correct cross-platform owner.
- "Existing evidence provides coverage" includes only locations where the real package export can already be traced to the host call and the Redux restoration chain can also be observed. A chain that has not been successfully traced cannot be frozen along with the desktop-side conclusion.

The review materials required the Desktop/Mobile comparison result, but "a comparison is required" does not mean "the two platforms are already equivalent." It is a work sequence before making a decision: reproduce first, then break down the differences. The initial draft placed these two things too close together, making it easy to read as saying that a comparison table alone would allow the window to be adjusted; the correction here is that the comparison result can only help locate the next conclusion and cannot by itself authorize an entry-point rearrangement.

## The Recheck Order Required at the Time

The recheck within the window was to proceed in the following order. The order itself is part of the decision, because the first person to propose an adjustment wanted to jump directly from the host entry point to a cross-platform conclusion, while the side retaining the entry point required the intermediate layers to be filled in first.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[package export] --> B[Host call]
  B --> C[Redux restoration chain]
  C --> D[Desktop/Mobile comparison]
  D --> E[Break into individually checkable conclusions]
```

The first step is to examine the real package export, rather than only the name near a host file. What must be confirmed here is the object the host actually receives; if the export does not match expectations, the later entry-point discussion has no basis.

The second step is to examine the host call. The existing desktop-side entry point can show only that the call site exists; it cannot show that the call's parameters, state reads, or restoration timing are the same as on the other side. The initial draft was overly optimistic about this layer, and during the later review it was no longer treated as complete proof that there was host-bindings.

The third step is to examine the Redux restoration chain. The most important thing to avoid in the freeze discussion is conflating "initially visible" with "still consistent after state restoration." If the restoration chain has not been successfully traced, even a similar surface result from Desktop/Mobile is not enough to decide whether the entry point should be adjusted consistently.

Only then comes the Desktop/Mobile comparison. Its output should be a set of small conclusions, such as whether a given export is read by the same type of host, whether a segment of the restoration passes through the same state, and whether the difference still exists. There is no need to write a large conclusion first; instead, we should prevent unconfirmed items from being put into generalizations such as "cross-platform alignment is complete."

## Judgments Retained from the Initial Draft

> Leave the current entry point unchanged for now and discuss it after the cross-platform picture is available.

This sentence was not deleted because it reflects the earliest working judgment and did in fact drive the decision to "retain first." But it is not precise enough. "Once the cross-platform picture is available" sounds as though only one result is missing, when what is actually missing is a traceable chain: from export to host, and then to restored state. The later addendum did not overturn the decision to retain the entry point; it only narrowed the meaning of this sentence.

> If the desktop can reproduce it, the mobile difference can wait until the next round.

This passage does not look well-founded now, but its original intent is retained. It treated desktop reproduction as a condition sufficient to close this round's scope. The view after review was that desktop reproduction can show only that the desktop-side behavior can be seen again; the Mobile comparison remains part of the freeze-material requirements. Without the comparison, "desktop is reproducible" should not be written as "the cross-platform issue has been isolated."

> The entry-point adjustment can ship with the version as a small fix.

This item was not adopted. The problem was not the words "small fix," but that no one at the time could clearly identify which segment of the restoration chain would be used as the comparison baseline after the adjustment. Without a baseline, an entry-point adjustment is not a small fix; it merely moves an unconfirmed item into the freeze window.

## Why the Window Was Not Adjusted

Adjusting the window appeared to reduce one later transition, but its compatibility cost could not be quantified at the time. The desktop host, the real package export, and Redux restoration are not a single point that can be replaced arbitrarily. As long as any one segment remains unchecked, it is impossible to determine which platform's behavior the change would alter, or to guarantee that the Desktop/Mobile comparison is still comparing the same thing.

Another proposal was to rename the entry point or move its location while leaving the behavior unchanged. This proposal likewise did not enter the current round. The freeze review was discussing the existing host-bindings entry point and the window arrangement, not providing an opportunity to clean up naming. Even if the behavior were assumed to remain unchanged, the export shape and restoration timing on which the host call depends would still need to be reconfirmed; before the evidence was complete, renaming or moving it would consume the same review attention.

Some people were also concerned that retaining the entry point would be misunderstood as making it the default solution. That concern is valid, so the decision explicitly retained the unadopted proposal and the reasons for opposing it: entry-point adjustment was not rejected as something that could never be done, but it was not allowed to pass directly on the basis of this round's materials. If it is proposed again next time, it cannot merely cite "this page once retained the entry point"; it must first provide a comparison along the same chain.

## Review Addendum

The most obvious change after review was that the Desktop/Mobile comparison was no longer treated as an item that could be checked off independently. Detached from the package export, host call, and Redux restoration chain, the comparison becomes a side-by-side description of two interfaces or two state segments; such a description can remind people to continue investigating, but it cannot determine the freeze boundary.

This also explains why only the covered scope was approved this round. "Coverage" here does not mean the amount of material, nor does it mean that each platform has its own explanation; it requires a specific path that can already be followed from the export to the host and through the restoration step. If a path has been found only on the desktop side, the record should say so; if the mobile side has not yet been verified, it should remain recorded as unverified for Mobile. Combining both sides under a vague "cross-platform" label would cause later judgments to lose their provenance.

The initial draft's tone made it feel as though retaining the entry point meant the work could immediately enter the freeze. It should now be read more narrowly: retaining the entry point is intended to prevent an unconfirmed adjustment from entering the window, not to shorten the comparison work. The comparison is still required within the window; its result simply will not automatically trigger an entry-point change.

## Matters Left Outside the Window

Entry-point adjustment remains an unadopted proposal, not an issue that has been erased. When it is raised again, it must at least answer three implementation-specific questions: what real package export is being compared; how the host actually invokes it on each platform; and which state segment is being compared after Redux restoration. If any one of the three is missing, the proposal should not be presented as "only changing the window."

No attribution to Mobile is provided here. The reason is not that Mobile is believed to have no differences, but that the materials at the time listed cross-platform comparison only as a requirement and did not provide a conclusion sufficient to attribute any behavior to the mobile implementation. Keeping this gap in the decision is more useful than filling it with an apparently reasonable attribution.

The desktop host-bindings entry point was also not registered as a permanent ownership assignment. Finding it initially through the desktop-side call name can show only that it was the starting point for this round's reproduction. # action-tiles Package Adjustment Entry-Point Notes

This record addresses a narrow handoff issue: after someone finds a public entry point through action-tiles, they need to know where the package owner adjustment first takes effect. The main risk is not too few search results, but too many. owner, export, and similar names appear in different files; they can show that an object passed through a location, but not necessarily that the location consumed the adjustment.

The initial draft made `devtools/registry/src/types.ts` the first stop, and that stays. At the time, it provided useful leads through the terms owner and export. The draft also placed too much weight on the package export list, as if following the list would lead to the adjustment point. After review, that assessment needs to change: the list only identifies package boundaries and public names. What actually determines the path is the direct call edge leading out of action-tiles.

```text
Public entry point of action-tiles
        |
        | Follow only one direct caller
        v
Corresponding name in the package export list
        |
        | Exclude same-name locations that only re-export
        v
First actual consumer of the package owner adjustment
```

## Start from the public entry point

At the entry point, first note the object exposed by action-tiles. Do not rush to explain which package it will ultimately affect. The task here is not to draw the full dependency graph, but to answer "what is the next hop?" If a caller is directly visible near the entry point, follow it first. If all you see is a re-export, that is still just an extension of the entry point; it does not mean you have found a consumer.

This is useful during handoff. The person taking over will often open the directory with the closest name first, then guess from filenames which implementation contains the owner adjustment. That approach mixes together same-name types, compatibility layers, and re-export locations. Work in the opposite order here: first confirm a direct call between action-tiles and a caller, then check that caller against the package export list. Record search hits without that edge only as signposts, not conclusions.

The type file is still a useful fixed point to return to when checking back. It does not make an ownership determination for the package owner; it provides a set of searchable public names and clues about boundaries. Once this layer is clear, the search narrows from "everywhere that mentions owner" to "places connected to this public name." That narrowing is more useful than continuing to add keywords.

## The list is not the endpoint

The package export list serves two purposes. First, it confirms that the object visible on the action-tiles side actually crosses a package boundary, rather than being a private name within the directory. Second, it lets you compare the direct caller and the public name side by side, so a file that merely shares the name does not get mistakenly connected to the chain.

The list itself is not a consumption point. A name can be listed, exported, and even appear again in several places, yet no one is handling the package owner adjustment. When reviewing a location like this, return to the direct caller: is it merely passing the object along, or is this where it hands the adjustment off to the next location? In the former case, keep looking ahead; only the latter is worth considering as a candidate. This distinction also explains why the initial draft could not stop at an export name alone.

Keep files that share the name but have no call edge in side notes. Sometimes they help confirm terminology; sometimes they are just similar names left over from earlier work. Calling them "possible entry points" would send the next person down the same wrong path. These signposts are not being deleted here, just removed from the main path.

## Stop at the first actual consumer

The main path ends at the first actual consumer of the package owner adjustment: continue along the confirmed direct calls, and when you first reach a location that needs to handle the adjustment, record that location and its relationship to the previous hop. That is enough to answer the entry-point question. Expanding the implementation beyond it will not make the entry point clearer; it will turn this page into code-reading notes for all of action-tiles.

To judge whether a consumer is "actual," do not look at filenames or count occurrences of owner. Check whether the previous hop actually sends the object here, and whether this location does more than re-export the same name. If a location contains only a declaration, a type description, or another re-export, it is still just material along the path. Only when it starts receiving the package owner adjustment is it the boundary this page is looking for.

This stopping point also leaves a necessary gap: this page does not stand in for confirmation of the specific arrangements after the first consumer. At a boundary that needs an explanation from another package, do not write guesses as call relationships. For the handoff, include the confirmed public entry point, direct caller, and corresponding export name. Let the other side fill in what they can answer from those three points in the location they maintain.

## Shortest route for a recheck

1. Take one object from the public entry point of action-tiles; do not start by expanding the search globally by owner name.
2. Confirm one direct caller; set aside results without a direct call edge.
3. Check the package boundary crossed by that object in the package export list, and revisit the name clues provided by `devtools/registry/src/types.ts`.
4. Continue along the confirmed calls until you first reach a location that handles the package owner adjustment.
5. Stop there. If another package needs to answer something later, leave only the specific question; do not fill in the downstream path with guesses.

This review did not remove the type file from the path or add an owner mapping table. What changed is the order used to determine the main path: direct call edges come first, the export list is used for verification, and the first consumer is where the entry-point question lands. The resulting record lets the next person retrace the path from action-tiles without treating every same-name file as an adjustment point.

# Postmortem: Release Evidence Archiving Discrepancy

## Observed behavior

During the release evidence archiving window, the results actually visible did not match the original plan. When it was discovered, the archived results were first reviewed item by item against the scheduled items, confirming that the discrepancy was in this window itself; this record does not expand it into a full release failure. The affected material was the archived material used at the time to verify release status; within the window, the comparison against the original plan could not be completed directly.

## Timeline

- First, the archived results were found to be inconsistent with the original plan; the specific cause was not determined at the time.
- A temporary recovery was then performed, returning the result to a state where it could be viewed and handled again, but this only showed that the temporary measure worked; it cannot be taken to mean that the root cause had been found.
- A Redux recovery sample was retained during the follow-up review. The investigation path went through `devtools/bindings/src/useFeatureFlagsToolProps.ts`, and the call name was also followed; this location was the investigation entry point at the time and should not be understood as permanent ownership.
- After handling was complete, the control point "Post-freeze exception approval" was added to the record: if the original plan needs to be changed during the freeze window, an exception approval must be recorded, and the result must then be brought back into the archive scope for verification.

## Assessment at the time

The early assessment favored the recovery path: because the result could still be used after the temporary recovery, it was initially handled along the Redux state-recovery path. This assessment was sufficient to support the recovery action at the time, but did not prove that the discrepancy was necessarily caused by Redux. In retrospect, the record should still retain this earlier assessment; the evidence from that time must not be replaced with a later framing.

## Unconfirmed items

This review did not establish why the discrepancy occurred, nor whether the recovery sample was merely incidental. There was not enough material left to distinguish whether the problem occurred in evidence generation, the archiving process, or result presentation. The temporary recovery restored usability within the window but did not close the investigation into the cause; therefore, this page is suitable as a historical record of that window, not as a step in the current release on-call procedure.

"Post-freeze exception approval" was a control point added later. It allows changes during the window to leave a trace that can be checked, but that does not mean the discrepancy has been explained.

```text
│  ├─ No: Record both sides' entry points and versions; stop with the submitter.

└─ Can the comparison table identify the differing item?
   ├─ Yes: Take that item to the corresponding owner.
   └─ No: New evidence or a new owner is needed; stop.
```

If the entry point or version isn't clearly documented, don't rely on successive reruns as a vote.
